Chemistry/General-Chemistry/01-Matter-an.title: 01 Matter and Measurement
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/01-Matter-an.content:
Overview
The scientific method is a set of procedures used to develop explanations of phenomena and possibly to predict additional phenomena. The 4 basic stages of the scientific method are:

Gathering date through observations and experiments.
Reducing the data to simple verbal or mathematic expression known as natural laws.
Offering a plausible explanation of the data through a hypothesis.
Testing the hypothesis through predictions and further experimentation, leading ultimately to conceptual model called a theory.

Matter is defined as anything that occupies space, possesses Mass and displays inertia. Composition refers to the component parts of a sample of matter and their relative proportions. Properties are the qualities that distinguish one sample of matter from another. They can be grouped into 2 broad categories: Physical Properties and Chemical Properties. Matter can undergo 2 types of changes:

Chemical Reactions are changes in composition.
Physical changes are changes in state or physical form and do not affect composition.

The basic building blocks of matter are called Atoms. Matter that is composed of a collection of a single type of atom is known as an Element. A sample of matter composed of 2 or more elements is known as a Compound. A Molecule is the smallest entity of a compound having the same proportions of the constituent atoms as does the compound as a whole. Collectively, elements and compounds compose the types of matter called Substances. Mixtures of substances can be classified as Homogeneous Mixture or Heterogeneous Mixture. The 3 State of Matter are Solid, Liquid, and Gas.
Chemistry is a quantitative science, meaning the chemical measurements are usually expressed in terms of a number and a unit. The scientific system of measurement, SI Units, involves seven base quantities. Mass describes a quantity of matter. Weight measures the Gravity Force of an object. The Temperature scales used by chemist are the Celsius and Kelvin scales.
Mass and Volume are Extensive Properties, they depend on the amount of matter in a sample. Density, the ratio of the mass of a sample to its volume, is an intensive property, a Property independent of the amount of matter sampled.
Measurements are subjects to systematic and random Errors. In making a series of measurements, the degree to which the measurements agree with one another is known as the Precision of the measurement, while the degree to which the measurements agree with the actual value is referred to as the accuracy of the measurement.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/01-Matter-an.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/01 Matter and Measurement/Accuracy vs Precision.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/01-Matter-an.title: Accuracy vs Precision
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/01-Matter-an.content:
Definition
Accuracy is how close a measurement to the true value. On the other hand, precision is how close repeated measurements are to each other.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/01-Matter-an.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/01 Matter and Measurement/Intensive vs Extensive Properties.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/01-Matter-an.title: Intensive vs Extensive Properties
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/01-Matter-an.content:

Intensive and extensive Properties are types of Physical Properties.
An Intensive property does not depend on the amount of Matter present in a Substance. Melting Point is an example of an intensive property.
On the other hand, Extensive property does depend on the amount of matter in a substance. Therefore it is considered additive. Mass is an example of an extensive property.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/01-Matter-an.title: Length
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/01-Matter-an.content:

Length is the measurement of distance between two points, indicating how long an object is from end to end.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/01-Matter-an.title: Liquid
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/01-Matter-an.content:
Definition
In a liquid, the Atoms or Molecules are usually separated by somewhat greater distances than in a Solid. Movement of these atoms or molecules gives a liquid its important Property, the ability to flow, covering the bottom and assuming the shape of its container.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/01-Matter-an.content:

Matter is any Substance with Mass and takes up space by having Volume.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/02-Atomic-Th.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/02 Atomic Theory/02 Atomic Theory.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/02-Atomic-Th.title: 02 Atomic Theory
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/02-Atomic-Th.content:
Overview
Modern chemistry began with 18th century discoveries leading to the formulation of 2 basic laws of chemical combination, the Conservation Of Mass and the Constant Composition Law. These discoveries led to Dalton’s Atomic Model- that Matter is Composed of indestructible particles called Atoms, that the atoms of an Element are identical to one another but different from atoms of all other elements, and that chemical Compounds are combinations of atoms of different elements.
The first clues to the structure of atoms came through cathode rays (Electrons). Key experiments were those that established the Mass to Charge ratio and then the charge on an electron. 2 important accidental discoveries made in the research were of X-rays and Radioactivity. The principal types of radiation emitted by radioactive Substances are Alpha Particles, Beta Particles and Gamma Rays.
Studies on the scattering of \alpha particles by thin metal foils led to the concept of the nuclear atom- a tiny, but massive, positively charged Nucleus surrounded by lightweight, negatively charged electrons. A more complete description of the nucleus was made possible by the discovery of Protons and Neutrons. An individual atom is characterized in terms of its Atomic Number, Z and Mass Number, A. The masses of individual atoms and their component parts are expressed in Atomic Mass Units.
All elements from Z = 1 to Z = 116 except for elements with Z = 113,115 have been characterized and all have been given a name and a chemical symbol. Atoms of the same element that differ in mass number are called Isotopes. The percent isotopic abundance of an isotope and the precise mass of its atoms can be established with a mass spectrometer. A special symbolism is used to represent the composition of an atom or an Ion.
The Atomic Mass of an element is a Weighted Average based on an assigned value of exactly 12 u for the isotope carbon 12. The weighted average is calculated from the experimentally determined atomic masses and percent abundances of the naturally occurring isotopes of the element.
The Periodic Table is an arrangement of the elements in horizontal rows called Periods and vertical columns called Groups. Each group consists of element with similar Physical and Chemical Properties. The elements can also be subdivided into broad categories. One categorization is that of Metals, Nonmetals, Metalloids and Noble Gases. Another is that of Main Group elements and Transition Elements.
The Avogadro’s Number N_A = 6.02214 \times 10^{23} mol^{-1}, represents the number of carbon-12 atoms in 12 g of carbon-12. Generally, it is the number of atoms or Molecules present in an amount known as one Mole of Substance. The mass of one mole of atoms of an element is called its Molar Mass.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/02-Atomic-Th.title: Atom
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/02-Atomic-Th.content:
Definition
Atom is a small particle that makes up Matter. Each different type of atom is the building block of a different chemical Element.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/02-Atomic-Th.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/02 Atomic Theory/Atomic Mass Units.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/02-Atomic-Th.title: Atomic Mass Units
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/02-Atomic-Th.content:

Atomic mass unit is a standard unit used to express Atomic Mass and Molecular Mass, defined as \frac{1}{12} of the Mass of a single carbon Atom. It equals 1.660539 \times 10^{-24} g.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/02-Atomic-Th.title: Atomic Mass
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/02-Atomic-Th.content:
Definition
The atomic mass of an Element is the average Mass of its Isotopes, weighted by how abundant they are in nature.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/02-Atomic-Th.title: Atomic Number
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/02-Atomic-Th.content:
Definition
The number of Protons in a given Atom is called the atomic number, Z. The number of Electrons on the atom is also equal to Z, because the atom is electrically neutral.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/02-Atomic-Th.title: Avogadro's Number
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/02-Atomic-Th.content:

N_A

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/02-Atomic-Th.title: Charge
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/02-Atomic-Th.content:
Definition
Electric charge is a fundamental Property of Matter, resulting from an inequality between Protons (positive) and Electrons (negative) within Atoms or Molecules. It dictates electromagnetic interactions, where like charges repel and opposite charges attract. Ions are charged species: Cations are positively charged (fewer electrons) and Anions are negatively charged (excess electrons).

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/02-Atomic-Th.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/02 Atomic Theory/Conservation Of Mass.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/02-Atomic-Th.title: Conservation Of Mass
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/02-Atomic-Th.content:
Definition
The total Mass of Substances present after a Chemical Reaction is the same as the total mass of substances before the reaction.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/02-Atomic-Th.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/02 Atomic Theory/Constant Composition Law.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/02-Atomic-Th.title: Constant Composition Law
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/02-Atomic-Th.content:
Definition
All samples of a Compound have the same Composition- the same proportion by Mass of the constituent Elements.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/02-Atomic-Th.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/02 Atomic Theory/Dalton's Atomic Model.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/02-Atomic-Th.title: Dalton's Atomic Model
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/02-Atomic-Th.content:
Definition
From 1803 to 1808, John Dalton used the 2 fundamental laws of chemical combination to describe the basis of an atomic theory. His theory involved three assumptions:

Each chemical Element is Composed of indivisible particles called Atoms. Atoms can be neither created nor destroyed during a Chemical Reaction.
All atoms of an element are alike in Mass and every other Property. Yet the atoms of an element are different from those of all other elements.
In each of their Compounds, different elements combine in a simple numerical ratio: one atom A to one of B (AB), or one atom A to 2 of B (AB_2).

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/02-Atomic-Th.title: Electron
Ion
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/02-Atomic-Th.content:
Definition
When an Atom lose or gain Electrons in a Chemical Reaction, the species formed are called Ions and carry net Charges.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/02-Atomic-Th.title: Isotope
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/02-Atomic-Th.content:
Definition
Atoms that have the same Atomic Number but different Mass Number are called Isotopes.
Of all the \ce{Ne} atoms on earth, 90.51% are \ce{^{20}_{10}Ne}. The percentages of \ce{^{21}_{10}Ne} and \ce{^{22}_{10}Ne} are 0.27% and 9.22%, respectively.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/02-Atomic-Th.title: Mass Number
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/02-Atomic-Th.content:
Definition
The total number of Protons and Neutrons in an Atom is called the mass number, A.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/02-Atomic-Th.title: Molar Mass
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/02-Atomic-Th.content:
Definition
The Mass of one Mole of Atoms is called the molar mass, M.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/02-Atomic-Th.title: Mole
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/02-Atomic-Th.content:
Definition
The SI Unit that describes an amount of Substance by relating it to a number of particles of that substance is called the mole. The number of elementary entities (Atoms, Molecules) in a mole is the Avogadro’s Number, N_A.
If a substance contains atoms of only a single Isotope, then
1 \text{mol} \, \ce{^{12}C} = 6.022 \times 10^{23} \, \ce{^{12}C} \,\text{atoms} = 12.0000 (g)

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/02-Atomic-Th.title: Molecular Mass
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/02-Atomic-Th.content:
Definition
Molecular mass is the Mass of a Molecule in atomic mass units. It is calculated by summing the Atomic Mass of each Atom in the molecule.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/02-Atomic-Th.title: Molecule
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/02-Atomic-Th.content:
Definition
A molecule is a group of Atoms held together by Chemical Bonds.

Nucleus

A nucleus is a small, central, positively Charged core inside an Atom, containing Protons and Neutrons.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/02-Atomic-Th.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/02 Atomic Theory/Rutherford's Atomic Model.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/02-Atomic-Th.title: Rutherford's Atomic Model
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/02-Atomic-Th.content:
Definition
The Rutherford atomic model, proposed by Ernest Rutherford in 1911, established that the Atom has a tiny, Dense, positively Charged Nucleus containing most of its Mass, surrounded by orbiting Electrons. The remainder of the atom is mostly empty space.
The magnitude of the positively charge is different for different atoms and is approximately half of the Atomic Mass of the Element. The atom as a whole is electrically neutral.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/02-Atomic-Th.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/02 Atomic Theory/Thomson's Atomic Model.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/02-Atomic-Th.title: Thomson's Atomic Model
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/02-Atomic-Th.content:
Definition
The Plum Pudding Model is a model of the Atom, proposed by J. J. Thomson in 1904.
It described the atom as a sphere of uniformly distributed, positively Charged “jelly” with negatively charged Electrons embedded within it.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/03-Chemical-.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/03 Chemical Compounds/03 Chemical Compounds.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/03-Chemical-.title: 03 Chemical Compounds
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/03-Chemical-.content:
Overview
The 2 main classes of chemical Compounds are Molecular Compounds and Ionic Compounds. The fundamental unit of a molecular compound is a Molecule and that of an ionic compound is a formula unit. A formula unit is the smallest collection of positively Charged Ions, called Cations and negatively charged ions, called Anions, that is electrically neutral overall. A Chemical Formula is a symbolic representation of a compound that can be written in several ways. If the formula has the smallest integral subscripts possible, it is an Empirical Formula. If the formula represents an actual molecule, it is a Molecular Formula. If the formula is written to show how individual Atoms are joined together  into molecules, it is a Structural Formula.
In this section , the concept of Atomic Mass is extended to Molecular Mass, the mass in Atomic Mass Units of a molecule of a molecular compound, and the formula mass, is the Mass in atomic mass units of a formula unit of an ionic compound. Likewise, the concept of Avogadro’s Number and the Molecule is now applied to compounds, with emphasis on quantitative applications involving the mass of a mole of compound, the Molar Mass.
The mass percent composition of a compound can be established from its formula. Conversely, a chemical formula can be deduced from the experimentally determined percent Composition of the compound. For Organic Compounds, this often involves Combustion analysis.
The Oxidation State of an atom is roughly related to the number of Electrons involved in the formation of a Chemical Bond between that atom and another one. Oxidation states are expressed as numbers assigned according to a Set of conversions.
Assigning names to the formulas of chemical compounds, nomenclature, is an important activity in chemistry. This topic is introduced in the section and applied to 2 broad categories:

Organic compounds, which are compounds formed by the elements carbon and hydrogen, often together with a few other Elements.
Inorganic compounds, a category that includes the remaining compounds.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/03-Chemical-.title: Anion
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/03-Chemical-.content:
Definition
An anion is a Nonmetal Atom in an Ionic Compound that becomes negative after losing an Electron.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/03-Chemical-.title: Cation
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/03-Chemical-.content:
Definition
A cation is a Metallic Atom in an Ionic Compound that becomes a positive Ion because it gained an Electron.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/03-Chemical-.title: Chemical Formula
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/03-Chemical-.content:
Definition
Chemical formulas represent Molecular Compounds with the Elements present and the relative number of Atoms of each element.
In the formula for Water, the constituent elements are denoted by their symbols. The relative number of atoms are indicated by subscripts.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/03-Chemical-.title: Combustion
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/03-Chemical-.content:
Definition
In combustion, a weighed sample of a Compound is burned in a stream of oxygen Gas. The Water Vapor and baron dioxide gas produces in the combustion are absorbed by appropriate Substances.
\ce{C_xH_yO_z} + \ce{O_2} \rightarrow x \ce{CO_2} + \frac{y}{2} \ce{H_2O}
After combustion, all the carbon Atoms in the sample are found in the \ce{CO_2}. All the hydrogen atoms are in the \ce{H_2O}.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/03-Chemical-.title: Empirical Formula
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/03-Chemical-.content:
Definition
An empirical formula is the simplest Chemical Formula fir a Compound. It shows the types of Atoms and their relative numbers. The subscripts are reduced to the their simplest Whole Number ratio.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/03-Chemical-.title: Ionic Compound
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/03-Chemical-.content:
Definition
An ionic compound is made up of positive and negative Ions joined together by electrostatic forces of attraction. The Atoms of Metal Elements tend to lose one or more Electrons to the Nonmetal atoms when they combine with them. It makes the compound into Cation and Anion.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/03-Chemical-.title: Molecular Compound
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/03-Chemical-.content:
Definition
A molecular compound is made up of Molecules, which typically consists of a small number of Nonmetal Atoms held together by Covalent Bonds. Molecular Compounds are represented by Chemical Formulas.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/03-Chemical-.title: Molecular Formula
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/03-Chemical-.content:
Definition
A molecular formula is based on an actual Molecule of a Compound. In some cases it is identical to the Empirical Formula and in other cases it is a multiple of the empirical formula.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/03-Chemical-.title: Oxidation State
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/03-Chemical-.content:
Definition
Oxidation state is the state of Charge, which is related to the number of Electrons that an Atom loses/gains when joining with other atoms in Compounds. Some rules for assigning oxidation states:

The oxidation state of an individual atom in a free Element is 0.
The sum of the oxidation state of all atoms in a Molecule is 0.
The sum of the oxidation state of all atoms in an Ion is equal to the charge on the ion.
In their compounds, the Group 1 Metals have an oxidation state of + 1 and the group 2 metals have + 2.
In its compounds, he oxidation state of fluorine is - 1.
In its compounds, hydrogen usually has an oxidation state of + 1.
In its compounds, oxygen usually has an oxidation state of - 2.
In two element compounds with metals, group 17 elements have an oxidation state of - 1; group 16 elements have - 2; and group 15 elements have - 3.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/03-Chemical-.title: Structural Formula
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/03-Chemical-.content:
Definition
A structural formula shows the order in which Atoms are bonded together in a Molecule and by what types of bonds.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/04-Chemical-.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/04 Chemical Reactions/04 Chemical Reactions.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/04-Chemical-.title: 04 Chemical Reactions
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/04-Chemical-.content:
Overview
Chemical Reactions are processes in which one or more starting Substances, the Reagents, form one or more new substances, the Products. A chemical reaction can be represented symbolically in a Chemical Equation, with Formulasof reagents on the left and formulas of products on the right. Reagents and products are separated by an arrow. The equation must be balanced. An equation is balanced by placing Stoichiometric Coefficients before formulas to signify that the total number of each kind of Atom is the same on each side of the equation. Reagents and products can be Solids, Liquids Gases or Aqueous Solution.
Stoichiometry comprises quantitative relationships based on Atomic and Molecular Mass, chemical formulas, balanced chemical equations, and related matters. Stoichiometric calculations usually require Molar Masses, Densities and percent Composition, along with other factors.
The Molality of a Solution is the amount of Solute (in Moles) per liter of solution. Molarity can be treated as a conversion factor between solution Volume and amount of solute. Molarity as conversion factor may be applied to individual solutions, to solutions that are mixed or diluted by adding more Solvent, and to reactions occurring in solution.
In some reactions, one of the reagents is completely consumed, while the other reagents remain in excess. The reagent that is completely consumed determines the amount of Product formed and is called the Limiting Reagent.
Stoichiometric calculations sometimes involve additional factors, including the reaction’s Actual Yield, the presence of By Products, and how the reaction or reactions proceed. For example, some reaction yield exactly the quantity of product calculated- the Theoretical Yield. When the actual yield is equal to the theoretical yield, the Percent Yield is 100 \%.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/04-Chemical-.title: Actual Yield
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/04-Chemical-.content:
Definition
The quantity of Product that is actually produced in a Chemical Reaction is called the actual yield.
In many reactions the actual yield almost exactly equals to the Theoretical Yield, and the reactions are said to be quantitative. In other reaction the actual yield is less than the theoretical yield. the reduced yield may occur for a few reasons:

The product of a reaction rarely appears in a pure form, and some product may be lost during the purification steps.
In many cases the Reagents may participate in reactions other than the one of interest, these are called side reactions.
If a reverse reaction occurs some of the expected product may react to reform the reagents.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/04-Chemical-.title: By Product
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/04-Chemical-.content:
Definition
A by product is the unintended Product of side Reactions.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/04-Chemical-.title: Chemical Equation
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/04-Chemical-.content:
Definition
A chemical equation is a way of representing a Chemical Reaction. In a chemical equation formulas for the Reagents are written on the let side and formulas for the Products are written on the right. The two sides of the equation are joined by an arrow (\rightarrow) . We say that the reagents yield the products.
In a balanced equation, the total number of Atoms of each Element present is the same on both sides.
==An equation can be balanced only by adjusting the Stoichiometric Coefficients of the formulas.==

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/04-Chemical-.title: Chemical Reaction
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/04-Chemical-.content:
Definition
A chemical reaction is a process in which one set of Substances, called Reagent is converted to a new set of substances called Product. A chemical reaction is the process by which a chemical change occurs. We need evidence before we can say that a reaction has occurred. Some of the types of physical evidence to look for:

a color change
formation of a Solid within a clear solution
evolution of a Gas
evolution or absorption of Heat

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/04-Chemical-.title: Consecutive Reactions
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/04-Chemical-.content:
Definition
In many cases a multistep process is necessary to yield a Product. Consecutive reactions are Chemical Reactions carried out one by one in sequence to Yield a final product.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/04-Chemical-.title: Limiting Reagent
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/04-Chemical-.content:
Definition
In some Chemical Reactions, one Reagent is completely converted into products by using an excess of all the other reagents. This reagent is called the limiting reagent, it determines the quantities of Products formed.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/04-Chemical-.title: Molarity
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/04-Chemical-.content:
Definition
The composition of a Solution can be described by molarity, which is defines as the amount of Solute, in Moles per liter of solution.
\text{molarity} = \frac{\text{amount of solute(in moles)}}{\text{amount of solution(in liters)}}
This can be written as:
c = \frac{n}{V}

























SymbolMeaningUnitscMolarity(\frac{\text{mol}}{L})namount of Solute(\text{mol})VVolume(L)
When calculating Concentration, we must determine the amount of solute in moles from the other quantities that can be measured, such as the Mass of the solute or the volume of a Liquid solute.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/04-Chemical-.title: Overall Reaction
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/04-Chemical-.content:
Definition
Often, we can combine a series of Chemical Equations for Consecutive Reactions to obtain a single equation to represent the overall reaction.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/04-Chemical-.title: Percent Yield
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/04-Chemical-.content:
Definition
The percent yield of Products in a Chemical Reaction is defines as the ratio of the Actual Yield and the Theoretical Yield.
\text{percent yield} = \frac{\text{actual yield}}{\text{theoretical yield}} \times 100 \%

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/04-Chemical-.title: Product
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/04-Chemical-.content:
Definition
In chemistry, a product is the specie formed from a Chemical Reaction.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/04-Chemical-.title: Reagent
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/04-Chemical-.content:
Definition
A reactant is a Substance that is consumed or altered during a Chemical Reaction. They are the starting materials, such as raw ingredients, that interact to form new Products.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/04-Chemical-.title: Simultaneous Reactions
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/04-Chemical-.content:
Definition
In simultaneous reactions, 2 or more Substances react independently of one another in separate Chemical Reactions occurring at the same time.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/04-Chemical-.title: Solute
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/04-Chemical-.content:
Definition
A solute is a component of a Solution, that dissolved in the Solvent.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/04-Chemical-.title: Solution
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/04-Chemical-.content:
Definition
A chemical solution is a homogeneous Mixture Composed of a Solute dissolved in a Solvent. These mixtures are uniform at the molecular level. We use the notation (aq), to describe a solution in which Liquid Water is the solvent.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/04-Chemical-.title: Solvent
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/04-Chemical-.content:
Definition
A solvent is a component of a Solution, that determines whether the solution exists as a Solid, Liquid or Gas.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/04-Chemical-.title: Stoichiometric Coefficients
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/04-Chemical-.content:
Definition
The coefficients required to balance a Chemical Equation are called stoichiometric coefficients. They are essential in relating the amounts of Reagents used and Products formed in a Chemical Reaction.
Here are some useful strategies for balancing equations:

If an Element occurs in only one Compound on each side of the equation, try balancing this element first.
When one of the reagents or products exists as a free element, balance this element last.
In some reactions, certain groups of Atoms remain unchanged. In such cases, balance these groups as a unit.
It is permissible to use fractional as well as integral numbers as coefficients. Lastly, clear the fractions by multiplying all coefficients by a common multiplier.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/04-Chemical-.title: Stoichiometry
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/04-Chemical-.content:
Definition
The term stoichiometry means to measure the Elements, but from a practical standpoint, using Stoichiometric Coefficients. It includes all the quantitative relationships involving Atomic Mass, Chemical Formula and Chemical Equation.
The coefficients in the chemical equation allow us to make statements such as:

2 Moles of \ce{H2O} are Produced for every 2 moles of \ce{H2} Reagent consumed.
2 moles of \ce{H2O} are produced for every 1 mole of \ce{O2} reagent consumed.
2 moles of \ce{H2} are consumed for every 2 moles of \ce{O2} reagent consumed.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/04-Chemical-.title: Theoretical Yield
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/04-Chemical-.content:
Definition
The theoretical yield of a Chemical Reaction is the calculated quantity of Product expected from given quantities of Reagents.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/05-Aqueous-R.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/05 Aqueous Reactions/05 Aqueous Reactions.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/05-Aqueous-R.title: 05 Aqueous Reactions
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/05-Aqueous-R.content:
Overview
Solutes in Aqueous Solution are characterized as Nonelectrolytes, which do not Produce Ions, or Electrolytes, which produce ions. Ionic Compounds produce ions by Dissociation whereas Molecular Compounds produce ions via Ionization. Weak Electrolytes ionize to a limited extend, and Strong Electrolytes dissociate or ionize almost completely into ions. In addition to the Molarity based on the solute as a whole, a Solution’s Concentration can be stated in terms of the molarities of the individual solute species present, Molecules and Ions.
Some Reactions in aqueous solution involve the combination of ions to yield a water-insoluble Solid, called a Precipitate. Precipitation reactions are generally represented by net ionic equations, a form in which only the reacting ions and solid precipitates are shown, and spectator ions are deleted.
According to the Arrhenius theory, a Substance that ionizes to produce \ce{H+} ions in aqueous solution is an Acid. It is a Strong Acid if the ionization goes essentially to completion and a Weak Acid if the ionization is limited. Similarly, a Base produces \ce{OH-} ions in aqueous solution and is either a Strong Base or a Weak Base, depending on the extent of the ionization. According to the Bronsted Lowry theory, in an Acid-Base Reaction, Protons are transferred from the acid (Proton Donor) to the base (Proton Acceptor). In an acid-base neutralization reaction, an  acid and a base react to form an ionic compound, a Salt. Water might also be a product.
In an Oxidation Reduction (redox) reaction certain Atoms undergo an increase in Oxidation State, a process called Oxidation. Other atoms undergo a decrease in oxidation state, or Reduction. An effective way to balance a redox Equation is to break down the reaction into separate half reactions, write and balance half equations for these half reactions, and recombine the balanced half equations into an Overall Reaction.
The Oxidant (oxidizing agent) is the key Reagent in an oxidation half reaction and is reduced in the redox reaction. The Reductant (reducing agent) is the key reagent in the reduction half reaction and is oxidized in the redox reaction.
A common laboratory technique applicable to Precipitation, Acid-Base, and redox reactions is Titration. The key point in a titration is the Equivalence Point, which can be observed with the aid of an Indicator. Titration data can be used to establish a solution’s Molarity, called standardization of a solution.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/05-Aqueous-R.title: Acid
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/05-Aqueous-R.content:
Definition
An acid is a Substance that provides hydrogen Ions \ce{H+} in Aqueous Solution.
There are Strong Acids and Weak Acids. Acid is a Proton Donor

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/05-Aqueous-R.title: Aqueous Solution
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/05-Aqueous-R.content:
Definition
An aqueous solution is a Solution for which Water is the Solvent. Whether or not an aqueous solution is a conductor of electricity depends on the nature of the Solute. Pure water contains so little Ions that it does not conduct electricity. Solutes that provide ions when dissolved in water are called Electrolytes. Solutes that does not provide ions are called Nonelectrolytes.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/05-Aqueous-R.title: Base
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/05-Aqueous-R.content:
Definition
A base is a Substance that Produces hydroxide Ions (\ce{OH-}) IN Aqueous Solution. There are Strong Bases and Weak Bases. A bases is a Proton Acceptor.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/05-Aqueous-R.title: Dissociation
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/05-Aqueous-R.content:
Definition
Dissociation refers to the separation of an entity into two or more. An Ionic Compound Produces Ions in Solution by dissociation.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/05-Aqueous-R.title: Electrolytes
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/05-Aqueous-R.content:
Definition
Electrolytes are essential minerals that carry an electric Charge and provide Ions when dissolved in Water. There are Strong Electrolyte and Weak Electrolyte.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/05-Aqueous-R.title: Indicator
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/05-Aqueous-R.content:
Definition
An indicator is a Substance used in Chemical Reactions mixture to Produce a color change.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/05-Aqueous-R.title: Ionization
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/05-Aqueous-R.content:
Definition
Ionization refers to the generation of one or more Ions. If a Molecular Compound Produces ions in Solution, it is by ionization.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/05-Aqueous-R.title: Neutralization Reaction
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/05-Aqueous-R.content:
Definition
A neutralization reaction is a Chemical Reaction between an Acid and a Base that forms an Aqueous Solution of an Ionic Compound called a Salt.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/05-Aqueous-R.title: Nonelectrolytes
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/05-Aqueous-R.content:
Definition
Nonelectrolytes are Substances that does not provide Ions when dissolved in Water.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/05-Aqueous-R.title: Oxidant
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/05-Aqueous-R.content:
Definition
In a Oxidation Reduction the Substance that makes it possible for some other substance to be Oxidized is called the oxidizing agent or oxidant. An oxidant contains an Element whose Oxidation State decreases in a redox reaction. The oxidant gains Electrons. In general, a substance with an element in one of its highest possible oxidation state is an oxidant.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/05-Aqueous-R.title: Oxidation Reduction
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/05-Aqueous-R.content:
Definition
Redox is a type of Chemical Reaction in which the Oxidation States of the Reagents change. Oxidation is the loss of Electrons while Reduction is the gain of electrons.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/05-Aqueous-R.title: Oxidation
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/05-Aqueous-R.content:
Definition
Oxidation is a process in which the Oxidation State of some Element increases by a loss of Electrons.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/05-Aqueous-R.title: Precipitate
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/05-Aqueous-R.content:
Definition
Some Metal Salts, are quite Soluble in Water. Precipitation reactions occur when Cations and Anions combine to Produce an insoluble Ionic Solid called a precipitate.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/05-Aqueous-R.title: Proton Acceptor
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/05-Aqueous-R.content:
Definition
A proton donor is a Substance, usually a Base that receives a hydrogen Ion \ce{H+} from another substance.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/05-Aqueous-R.title: Proton Donor
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/05-Aqueous-R.content:
Definition
A proton donor is a Substance, usually Acid that releases a hydrogen Ion \ce{H+} to another substance.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/05-Aqueous-R.title: Reductant
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/05-Aqueous-R.content:
Definition
In the Oxidation Reduction reaction, the Substance that causes some other substance to be Reduced is called the reducing agent or reductant. The reductant contains an Element whose Oxidation State increases in a redox reaction. The reductant loses Electrons. If the substance with the element is in one of its lowest possible oxidation states, the substance is a reductant.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/05-Aqueous-R.title: Reduction
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/05-Aqueous-R.content:
Definition
Reduction is a process in which the Oxidation State of some Element decreases due to a gain of Electrons

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/05-Aqueous-R.title: Salt
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/05-Aqueous-R.content:
Definition
A salt is the Product of a Neutralization Reaction. Salt is an Ionic Compound.
\ce{HCl(aq) + NaOH(aq) -> NaCl(aq) + H2O(l)}
The \ce{H+} Ions from the Strong Acid and the \ce{OH-} ions from the Base combine to form Water.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/05-Aqueous-R.title: Strong Acid
Strong Base
Strong Electrolyte
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/05-Aqueous-R.content:
Definition
A strong electrolyte is a Substance that is completely Ionized in Aqueous Solution. All of the dissolved Solute exists as Ions.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/05-Aqueous-R.title: Weak Acid
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/05-Aqueous-R.content:
Definition
A weak acid is a Molecular Compound that has a weak tendency for Producing \ce{H+} Ions. A weak acid is incompletely Ionized in Aqueous Solution. Most Acids are weak acids.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/05-Aqueous-R.title: Weak Base
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/05-Aqueous-R.content:
Definition
A Base that is incompletely Ionized in Aqueous Solution is a weak base. Most basic Substances are weak bases.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/05-Aqueous-R.title: Weak Electrolyte
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/05-Aqueous-R.content:
Definition
A weak electrolyte is only partially Ionized in Aqueous Solution. Only some of the dissolved Solute is converted into Ions.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/06-Gases/06-.title: 06 Gases
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/06-Gases/06-.content:
Overview
A Gas is described in terms of its Pressure, Temperature, Volume and amount. Gas pressure is most readily measured by comparing it with the pressure exerted by a Liquid column, usually mercury. The pressure exerted in a barometer and called the barometric pressure is equal to the prevailing pressure of the atmosphere. Other gas pressures can be measured with a manometer. Pressure can be expressed in a variety of units, including the SI Unitspascal (Pa) and kilopascal (kPa). also commonly used are bar, millimeter of mercury (mmHg), torr, atmosphere (atm).
The most common simple gas laws are Boyle’s Law relating gas pressure and volume. Charles’s Law relating gas volume and temperature. There is also Avogadro’s Law, relating volume and amount of gas. Some important ideas that originate from the simple gas laws are the Kelvin scale of temperature, and the STP.
The simple gas laws can be combined into the Ideal Gas Equation, PV = nRT, where R is the Gas Constant. A gas whose behavior can be predicted with this equation known as Ideal Gas. The ideal gas equation can solve for any one of the variables when all the others are known. The General Gas Equation is useful variant of the ideal gas equation for describing the behavior of a gas when certain variables are held constant and other are allowed to change. An important application of the ideal gas equation is its use in determining Molecular Masses and gas Densities.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/06-Gases/Avo.title: Avogadro's Law
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/06-Gases/Avo.content:
Definition
At a fixed Temperature and Pressure, the Volume of a Gas is directly proportional to the amount of gas in Moles
V \propto n
or V = kn
where k is a constant

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/06-Gases/Boy.title: Boyle's Law
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/06-Gases/Boy.content:
Definition
For a fixed amount of Gas at a constant Temperature, the gas Volume is inversely proportional to the gas Pressure.
P \propto \frac{1}{V} or
PV=a
where a is a constant.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/06-Gases/Cha.title: Charles's Law
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/06-Gases/Cha.content:
Definition
The Volume of a fixed amount of Gas at constant Pressure is directly proportional to the Kelvin Temperature.
V \propto T
or
V = bT
where b is a constant.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/06-Gases/Gas.title: Gas Constant
Gas
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/06-Gases/Gas.content:
Definition
A gas is a state of matter with no fixed Volume or shape. It is a compressible form of fluid, unlike a Liquid. A pure gas consists of individual Atoms (Noble Gas) or Molecules (for example \ce{O2}). Gases diffuse into one another. 4 Properties determine the physical behavior of a gas:

the amount of the gas (in Moles)
the volume of the gas
the Temperature of the gas
the Pressure of the gas

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/06-Gases/Gen.title: General Gas Equation
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/06-Gases/Gen.content:
Definition
The general gas equation is the general case of the Ideal Gas Equation when a gas has two different sets of conditions. The ideal gas equation is applied twice: to the initial condition and the final condition.
P_i V_i = n_i R T_i , \, \, P_f V_f = n_f R T_f
when isolating R and comparing:
\frac{P_i V_i}{n_i T_i} = \frac{P_f V_f}{n_f T_f}

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/06-Gases/Ide.title: Ideal Gas Equation
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/06-Gases/Ide.content:
Definition
When combining Boyle’s Law, Charles’s Law and Avogadro’s Law into one equation, we get the ideal gas equation.
V \propto \frac{nT}{P}
or
P = R\frac{nT}{p} \\
PV = nRT
\end{array}$$

where $R$ is called the [[Gas Constant]]
A [[Gas]] whose behavior conforms to the ideal gas equation is called an [[Ideal Gas]].

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/06-Gases/Ide.title: Ideal Gas
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/06-Gases/Ide.content:
Definition
An ideal gas is a theoretical Gas that obeys the Ideal Gas Equation.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/06-Gases/Kin.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/06 Gases/Kinetic Molecular Theory of Gases.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/06-Gases/Kin.title: Kinetic Molecular Theory of Gases
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/06-Gases/Kin.content:
Definition
The kinetic molecular theory of gases is a theory that follows this rules:

A Gas is composed of a very large number of Atoms or Molecules in constant, random, straight line motion.
Molecules of a gas are separated by great distances. The gas is mostly empty space.
Molecules Collide only fleetingly with one another and with the walls of their container, and most of the time molecules are not colliding.
There are assumed to be no Forces between molecules except very briefly during collisions. That is, each molecule acts independently of all the others and is unaffected by their presence, except during collisions.
Individual molecules may gain or lose Energy as a result of collisions. In a collection of molecules at constant Temperature the total Energy remains constant.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/06-Gases/Pre.title: Pressure
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/06-Gases/Pre.content:
Definition
Pressure is defines as a Force per unit area.
P(Pa) = \frac{F(N)}{A(m^2)}
Because it is difficult to measure the total force of a gas, it is measured indirectly, by comparing it with a Liquid pressure. Consider a liquid with Density d, contained in a cylinder with cross sectional area A filled to a height h.
P = \frac{F}{A} = \frac{W}{A} = \frac{gm}{A}
The Mass of a liquid is the product of its Volume  and density:
m = Vd
And the volume of a cylinder is the product of its volume and height:
V = hA
Substituting:
P = \frac{gm}{A} = \frac{gVd}{A} = \frac{ghAd}{A} = ghd
Variables

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/06-Gases/STP.title: STP
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/06-Gases/STP.content:
Definition
Standard conditions of temperature and pressure or STP is the standard for comparing different Gases. The standard Temperature for gases is taken to be 0^\circ\mathrm{C} = 273.15 \mathrm{K}, and the standard Pressure is 1 bar = 100 kPa = 10^5 Pa.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/07-Thermoche.title: 07 Thermochemistry
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/07-Thermoche.content:
Overview
The subject of a thermochemical study is broken into the System of interest and the portions of the universe with which the system may interact, the Surroundings. An Open System can exchange both Energy and Matter with its surroundings. A Closed System can exchange only energy and not matter. An Isolated System can exchange neither energy nor matter with its surroundings. Energy is the capacity to do Work and work is performed when a Force acts through a distance. Energy can be characterized as Kinetic Energy (energy associated with matter in motion) or Potential Energy (energy resulting from the position or Composition of matter). Kinetic energy associated with random molecular motion is called Thermal Energy.
Heat is energy transferred between system and its surroundings as a result of a Temperature difference between the 2. In some cases, heat can be transferred at constant temperature, as in a change in State of Matter in the system. A quantity of heat is the Product of the Heat Capacity of the system and the temperature change. In turn, heat capacity is the product of Mass and Specific Heat Capacity, the amount of heat required to change the temperature of one gram of Substance by one degree Celsius. Alternatively, heat capacity is the product of amount (in Moles) and Molar Heat Capacity, the quantity of heat required to increase the temperature of one mole of substance by 1 degree. Historically, the unit for measuring heat has been the Calorie, but the SI Units of heat is the joule. Energy transfers between a system and its surroundings must conform to the Law of Conservation of Energy, meaning that all heat lost by a system is gained by its surroundings.
In a Chemical Reaction, a change in the Chemical Energy associated with the Reagents and products may appear as heat. The Heat of Reaction is the quantity of heat exchanged between a system and its surroundings when the reaction occurs at a constant temperature. In an Exothermic Reaction, heat is given off by the system. In a Endothermic Reaction, the system absorbed heat.
In some reactions an energy transfer between a system and its surroundings occurs as work. This is commonly the work involved in the expansion or compression of Gases and is called Pressure Volume Work.
Internal Energy, U is the total energy in a system. The First Law of Thermodynamics relates changes in the internal energy of a system \Delta U to the quantities of heat q and work w exchanged between the system and its surroundings. The relationship is \Delta U = q + w and requires that a Set of sign conversions be consistently followed. A State Function has a value that depends only on the exact condition or state in which a system is found and not on how that state was reached. Internal energy is a state function. A path-dependent function, such as heat or work, depends on how a change in a system is achieved. A change that is accomplished through an infinite number of infinitesimal steps is a Reversible Process, whereas a change accomplished in one step or a finite series of steps is an Irreversible Process.
With work limited to pressure-volume work, the heat transferred in a constant volume process is equal to the internal energy change. For constant pressure processes, a more useful function is Enthalpy H, defined as the internal energy of a system plus the pressure volume product. PV. The heat transferred in a constant pressure process is equal to the enthalpy change \Delta H of the system. Most often, a heat of reaction is reported as a \Delta _r H value, the enthalpy change per mole of reaction. A substance under a pressure of 1 (bar) = 10^5 (Pa) and at the temperature of interest is said to be in its Standard State. If the reagents and products of a reaction are in their standard states, the enthalpy change in a reaction is called the standard Enthalpy of Reaction and is designated as \Delta _r H^{\circ}. Enthalpy changes can be represented schematically through enthalpy diagrams.
Often an unknown \Delta _r H value can be established indirectly through Hess’s Law, which states that an overall enthalpy change is the sum of the enthalpy changes of the individual steps leading to the overall process.
By arbitrarily assigning an enthalpy of 0 to the reference forms of the Elements in their standard states, the enthalpy change in the formation of a Compound from its elements becomes a Standard Enthalpy of Formation \Delta _f H^{\circ}.
A process that proceeds without external intervention is said to be Spontaneous Process. A Nonspontaneous Process cannot occur without externa intervention. If a process is spontaneous in one direction, then it is nonspontaneous in the reverse direction.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/07-Thermoche.title: Calorie
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/07-Thermoche.content:
Definition
The quantity of Heat required to change the Temperature of one gram of Water by one degree Celsius is called calorie. It is a small unit of Energy.
1 cal = 4.184J

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/07-Thermoche.title: Chemical Energy
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/07-Thermoche.content:
Definition
Chemical energy is the Energy associated with chemical bonds and intermolecular attractions. If we think of a Chemical Reaction as a process in which some chemical bonds are broken and formed,, that we expect the chemical energy of a System to change.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/07-Thermoche.title: Closed System
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/07-Thermoche.content:
Definition
A closed system is a System that can exchange Energy, but not Matter with its Surroundings.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/07-Thermoche.title: Endothermic Reaction
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/07-Thermoche.content:
Definition
An endothermic reaction is a Chemical Reaction that absorbs Thermal Energy from its Surroundings, causing a decrease in Temperature in the System. For an endothermic reaction, the Heat of Reaction is positive (q_{rxn} > 0).

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/07-Thermoche.title: Enthalpy of Reaction
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/07-Thermoche.content:
Definition
The enthalpy of reaction is the Heat absorbed or released during a Chemical Reaction at constant Pressure. It represents the difference between the total Enthalpy of Products and Reagents
\Delta H_{rxn} = H_{products} - H_{Reagents}
The enthalpy of reaction changes sign when a a process is Reversed.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/07-Thermoche.title: Enthalpy
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/07-Thermoche.content:
Definition
Imagine a System with constant Volume, because of that no Work is done. W = -P_{ext} \Delta V = 0If the Heat transferred for this constant volume process is denoted as q_V, than by the First Law of Thermodynamics:
\Delta U = q_V
Now, imagine a system with constant Pressure, if the heat transferred for this constant pressure process is denoted as q_P:
\Delta U = q_P -P_{ext} \Delta V \\
U_f - U_i = q_P -P_fV_f + P_iV_i \\
q_P = (U_f + P_fV_f) - (U_i + P_iV_i)
\end{array}$$
The right side of the expression is made up with [[State Function]], so it as a whole must be a state function. This state function is called the **enthalpy**, $H$, and is the sum of the [[Internal Energy]] and the pressure-volume product: $H = U + PV$.
$$\Delta H = H_f - H_i = q_P$$
Substituting into the [[First Law of Thermodynamics]]:
$$\Delta U = \Delta H - P \Delta V$$

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/07-Thermoche.title: Exothermic Reaction
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/07-Thermoche.content:
Definition
An exothermic reaction is a Chemical Reaction that Produces a Temperature increase in an Isolated System or, in a nonisolated system, gives off Heat to the Surroundings. For an exothermic reaction, the Heat of Reaction is negative (q_{rxn} < 0).

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/07-Thermoche.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/07 Thermochemistry/First Law of Thermodynamics.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/07-Thermoche.title: First Law of Thermodynamics
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/07-Thermoche.content:
Definition
The first law of thermodynamics is a relationship between Heat, Work and the changes in Internal Energy in a System.
\Delta U = q + W
An Isolated System is unable to exchange heat or work with its Surroundings, so that the energy of an isolated system is constant.
Any energy entering the system is positive. If heat is absorbed by the system, q > 0. If work is done on the system, W > 0.
Any energy leaving the system is negative. If heat is given off by the system, q < 0. If work is done by the system, W < 0.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/07-Thermoche.title: Heat Capacity
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/07-Thermoche.content:
Definition
The quantity of Heat required to change the Temperature of a System by one degree is called the heat capacity. Represented by the symbol C.
C = \frac{q}{\Delta T}
Heat capacity depends on whether the system is heated at constant Pressure or at constant Volume. To distinguish between them, the symbols C_p and C_V are used.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/07-Thermoche.title: Heat of Reaction
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/07-Thermoche.content:
Definition
A heat of reaction, q_{rxn} , is the quantity of Heat exchanged between a System and its Surroundings when a Chemical Reaction occurs within the system at constant Temperature. If a reaction occurs in an Isolated System, the reaction Produces a change in the Thermal Energy of the system. The temperature either increases or decreases.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/07-Thermoche.title: Heat
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/07-Thermoche.content:
Definition
Heat is the Energy transferred between a System and its Surroundings as a result of a Temperature difference. Energy that passes from a warmer body to a colder body is transferred as heat. At the molecular level, Molecules of the warmer body, through collisions, lose Kinetic Energy to those of the colder body. Thermal Energy is transferred until the average molecular kinetic energies of the two bodies become the same.
At constant Pressure:
q = C_p \Delta T = n C_{p,m} \Delta T = mc_p \Delta T

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/07-Thermoche.title: Hess's Law
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/07-Thermoche.content:
Definition
If a process occurs in stages, the Enthalpy change for the overall process is the sum of the enthalpy changes for the individual stages.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/07-Thermoche.title: Internal Energy
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/07-Thermoche.content:
Definition
The internal energy, denoted as U is the total Energy, both Kinetic Energy and Potential Energy in a System, including the kinetic energy of Molecules, molecular rotations and vibrations,, energy stored in chemical bonds,, inter molecular attractions and the energy associated with Electrons in Atoms.
A system contains only internal energy, and does not contain energy in the form of Heat or Work.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/07-Thermoche.title: Irreversible Process
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/07-Thermoche.content:
Definition
An irreversible process involves finite amounts of intermediate states. Changes produced in the System or Surroundings cannot be undone by reversing the steps.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/07-Thermoche.title: Isolated System
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/07-Thermoche.content:
Definition
An isolated system is a System that does not interact with its Surroundings.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/07-Thermoche.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/07 Thermochemistry/Law of Conservation of Energy.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/07-Thermoche.title: Law of Conservation of Energy
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/07-Thermoche.content:
Definition
In interactions between a System and its Surroundings, the total Energy remains constant. Energy is neither created nor destroyed. When applied to the exchange of Heat, this means that:
q_{\text{system}} + q_{\text{surroundings}} = 0

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/07-Thermoche.title: Molar Heat Capacity
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/07-Thermoche.content:
Definition
The molar heat capacity at constant Pressure, denoted as C_{p,m} is the quantity of Heat required to raise the Temperature of one Mole of a Substance by one degree under the condition of constant pressure.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/07-Thermoche.title: Nonspontaneous Process
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/07-Thermoche.content:
Definition
A nonspontaneous process is a process in a System, that will not occur unless some action from its Surroundings is continuously applied.
If a process is Spontaneous, the Reverse Process is nonspontaneous.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/07-Thermoche.title: Open System
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/07-Thermoche.content:
Definition
An open system is a System that freely exchanges Energy and Matter with its Surroundings.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/07-Thermoche.title: Pressure Volume Work
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/07-Thermoche.content:
Definition
Pressure volume work, or P - V Work is the Energy transferred when a System (usually Gas) expands or compresses against an external Pressure.
W = - \frac{Mg}{A} \Delta h A = - P_{ext} \Delta V

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/07-Thermoche.title: Reversible Process
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/07-Thermoche.content:
Definition
A reversible process involves an infinite number if intermediate states, with the System variables changing from their initial values to their final values by infinitesimally small amounts.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/07-Thermoche.title: Specific Heat Capacity
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/07-Thermoche.content:
Definition
The constant Pressure specific heat capacity, denoted as c_p is the quantity of Heat required to change the Temperature of one gram of Substance by one degree.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/07-Thermoche.title: Spontaneous Process
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/07-Thermoche.content:
Definition
A spontaneous process is a process that occurs in a System left to itself. Once started, no action from its Surroundings is necessary to make the process continue.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/07-Thermoche.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/07 Thermochemistry/Standard Enthalpy of Formation.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/07-Thermoche.title: Standard Enthalpy of Formation
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/07-Thermoche.content:
Definition
The standard enthalpy of formation, \Delta _f H^{\circ}, is the change of Enthalpy when exactly one Mole of a Compound is formed from its constituent Elements in their Standard State.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/07-Thermoche.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/07 Thermochemistry/Standard Enthalpy of Reaction.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/07-Thermoche.title: Standard Enthalpy of Reaction
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/07-Thermoche.content:
Definition
The standard enthalpy of reaction, \Delta _r H^{\circ}, is the Heat absorbed or released during a Chemical Reaction when Reagents in their Standard States convert to Products in their standard states, based on molar amounts in a balanced Chemical Equation.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/07-Thermoche.title: Standard State
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/07-Thermoche.content:
Definition
A standard state is a reference point used to calculate thermodynamic Properties, defined as the most stable physical form of a Substance at a specific Pressure of 10^5 Pa and room temperature. It ensures consistency in calculating Enthalpy, Entropy, and Gibbs Energy.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/07-Thermoche.title: State Function
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/07-Thermoche.content:
Definition
Any Property that has a unique value for a specific state of a System is said to be a state function. Pressure, Temperature, Density, Internal Energyare examples of state functions.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/07-Thermoche.title: Surroundings
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/07-Thermoche.content:
Definition
The surroundings are that part of the universe outside the System with which the system interacts.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/07-Thermoche.title: System
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/07-Thermoche.content:
Definition
A system is the part of the universe chosen for study. There are 3 types of systems: The Open System, Closed System and Isolated System.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/07-Thermoche.title: Thermal Energy
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/07-Thermoche.content:
Definition
Thermal energy is the internal Energy of an object due to the Kinetic Energy of its moving Atoms and Molecules. Thermal energy is proportional to the Temperature of a System.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/08 Electrons in Atoms/08 Electrons in Atoms.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.title: 08 Electrons in Atoms
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.content:
Overview
Electromagnetic Radiation is a type of Energy transmission in the form of a Wave. The waves of electromagnetic radiation are characterized by an Amplitude, the maximum height of wave crests and maximum depth of wave throughs, a Wavelength, \lambda, the distance between wave crests and Frequency, \nu, which signifies how often the fluctuations occur. Frequency is measured in hertz, (Hz), cycles per second. Wavelength and frequency are related by the equation: c = \lambda \nu, where c is the Speed of Light. The wave character of electromagnetic radiation means that the waves can be dispersed into individual components of different wavelengths, a Diffraction pattern, by striking a closely grooved surface.
The study of electromagnetic radiation emitted from hot objects led to Plank’s theory, which states that quantities of energy can have only certain values, with the smallest unit of energy being that of a Quantum. The energy of a quantum is given by the equation: E = h \nu, where h is Planck’s Constant. Einstein’s interpretation of the Photoelectric Effect, the ability of light to eject Electrons when striking certain surfaces, led to a new interpretation of electromagnetic radiation: Light has a particle-like nature in addition to its wave-like Properties. Light particles are called Photons. The energy of a photon is related to the frequency of the radiation by: E_{\text{photon}} = h \nu.
Light emitted from excited Atoms and Ions consists of a limited number of wavelength components, which can be dispersed by a prism to produce Atomic Spectra.
The Energy Level of the hydrogen atom depend of a quantum number, n, which can take on the values n = 1,2,3,... The lowest energy state, with n = 1, is called the Ground State. Levels with n > 1 are called Excited States. The state with quantum number n = \infty corresponds to an Ionized hydrogen atom. The allowed energy levels can be represented using an energy-level diagram. Transitions between various levels are accompanied by either the absorption or emission of photons, the energies of which match the magnitude of the energy difference, |\Delta E|, between the 2 levels.
Louis de Broglie postulated Wave-Particle Duality in which particles of Matter such as Protons and electrons would at times display a wave-like properties. Because of an inherent uncertainty of the position and Momentum of a wave-like particle, Heisenberg postulated that we cannot simultaneously know a subatomic particle’s precise momentum and its position, a proposition referred to as the Heisenberg Uncertainty Principle.
The application of the concept of wave-particle duality requires that we view the electron in a System in terms of a Wave Function that corresponds to a Standing Wave within the boundary of the system. Application of these ideas to a particle in a one-dimensional box shows that at the lowest energy level, the energy of the particle is nonzero that is, the system has a Zero Point Energy.
The solution of the Schrodinger Equation for the hydrogen atom provides wave functions called Orbitals, which are the product of a Radial Wave Function, R(r), and an Angular Wave Function, \Upsilon(\theta,\phi). The three quantum numbers arising from the Schrodinger wave equation are the principal quantum number, n the orbital angular momentum quantum number, \ell, and the magnetic quantum number, m_{\ell}. All orbitals with the same value of n are in the same Principal Electronic Shell, and all orbitals with the same value of n and \ell are in the same Subshell. The orbitals with different values of \ell are designated s,p,d,f. Orbitals in the same subshell of a hydrogen-like species have the same energy and said to be degenerate.
Stern and Gerlach demonstrated that electrons possess a quality called Electron Spin. The electron spin quantum number, m_s , takes the value of +\frac{1}{2} or -\frac{1}{2}.
The wave function of a multielectron atom can be approximated as a superposition of orbitals, each of which is qualitatively similar to a hydrogen-like orbital. In multielectron atoms, orbitals with different values of \ell are not degenerate. The loss of degeneracy within the principal shell is explained in terms of the different Effective Nuclear Charge, Z_{\text{eff}}, experienced by electrons in different subshells.
Electron Configuration describes how the electrons are distributed among the various orbitals in principal shells and subshells of an atom. Electrons fill orbitals in a way that minimizes the total energy of an atom. The Pauli Exclusion Principle states that a maximum of 2 electrons may occupy an orbital. Hund’s Rule says that when degenerate orbitals are available, electrons initially occupy these orbitals singly with parallel spins. Electron configurations are represented by either expanded or condensed Orbital Diagram. The Aufbau Process is used to assign electron configurations to the Elements of the Periodic Table. Electrons added to the shell of highest quantum number in the Aufbau process are called Valence Electrons.
Elements in the same Group of the periodic table have similar electron configurations. Group 1 and 2 correspond to the s block with filled or partially filled valence-shell s orbitals. Groups 13-18 correspond to the p block with filled or partially filled valence-shell p orbitals. The d block corresponds to groups 3-12 as the n-1 energy level is being filled- that is, having filled or partially filled d orbitals. In the f block elements, are also called the lanthanides and actinides, the n-2 shell fills with electrons, that is, they have filled or partially filled f orbitals.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/08 Electrons in Atoms/Amplitude.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.title: Amplitude
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.content:
Definition
The maximum height of the Wave above the center line or the maximum depth below is called the amplitude.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/08 Electrons in Atoms/Atomic Orbital.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.title: Atomic Orbital
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.content:
Definition
An atomic orbital is a function describing the location and wave-like behavior of an Electron in an Atom. Each orbital in an atom is characterized by a set of values of 3 Quantum numbers:

The principal quantum number, n, which may have only a positive, non zero integral value. n = 1,2,3,...
The orbital Angular Momentum quantum number, \ell, which may be zero or a positive integer but not larger than n. \ell = 0,1,2,...,n-1
The magnetic quantum number, m_{\ell}, which may be a negative or positive integer including zero, and ranging from -\ell to +\ell. m_{\ell} = -\ell, -\ell+1, ...,-1,0,1,...,\ell-1,\ell

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/08 Electrons in Atoms/Atomic Spectra.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.title: Atomic Spectra
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.content:
Definition
The atomic spectra are the unique Sets of light Frequencies emitted or absorbed by Elements and acting as elemental fingerprints due to the Quantized Electron Energy Levels. When electrons drop to lower energy levels, they emit light (emission spectrum), and when they absorb energy, they move to higher levels (absorption spectrum).

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/08 Electrons in Atoms/Diffraction.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.title: Diffraction
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.content:
Definition
White light contains all the colors of the rainbow. The colors differ in Wavelength and Frequency. The dispersion of different wavelength components of a light beam through the interference produced by reflection from  a grooved surface is called diffraction.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/08 Electrons in Atoms/Effective Nuclear Charge.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.title: Effective Nuclear Charge
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.content:
Definition
The effective nuclear charge, Z_{\text{eff}} , is the net positive Charge experienced by an Electron in a multielectron Atom, always lower than the Atomic Number Z, due to the shielding effect of inner-shell electrons. It determines Periodic Trends such as Atomic Radius, Ionization Energy and Electronegativity.
Z_{\text{eff}} = Z - S S is the shielding constant (roughly the number of inner/core electrons).
Z_{\text{eff}} increases across a Period from left to right because the number of Protons increases while shielding the inner electrons remains relatively constant, pulling Valence Electrons closer.
Z_{\text{eff}} increases only slightly down a Group, as the increased shielding from additional inner shells roughly cancels out the increase nuclear charge.
Electrons with higher Z_{\text{eff}} are more tightly bound to the Nucleus, causing smaller atomic radii and higher ionization energies.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/08 Electrons in Atoms/Electromagnetic Radiation.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.title: Electromagnetic Radiation
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.content:
Definition
Electromagnetic radiation is a form of Energy transmission in which electric and magnetic fields are propagated as Waves through empty space or through a medium.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/08 Electrons in Atoms/Electron Configuration.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.title: Electron Configuration
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.content:
Definition
The electron configuration of an Atom is the designation of how Electrons are distributed among the Orbitals in Principal shells and Subshells.
Rules for assigning electrons to orbitals:

Electrons occupy orbitals in a way that minimizes the Energy of the atom. Also known as Pauli exclusion principle. 1s,2s,2p,3s,3p,4s,3d,4p,5s,4f,5d,6p,7s,5f,6d,7p
Only two electrons may occupy the same orbital, and these electrons must have two opposite Spins.
When orbitals of identical energy, are available, electrons initially occupy these orbitals singly and with parallel spins. Also known as Hund’s Rule.

To write electron configurations we’ll use the Aufbau process. Assign electron configurations to the Elements in order of increasing Atomic Number. To proceed from one atom to the next, we add a Proton and some Neutrons to the Nucleus and then describe the orbital into which the added electron goes.

Z = 1, H. The lowest energy state for the electron is the 1s orbital. The electron configuration is 1s^1.
Z = 2, He. A second electron goes into the s1 orbital and the two electrons have opposing spins, 1s^2.
Z = 3, Li. The third electron cannot fit in the s1 orbital. It goes to the lowest energy orbital available, 2s. The electron configuration is 1s^2 2s^1.
Z = 4, Be. Configuration is 1s^2 2s^2.
Z = 5, B. Now the next orbital, 2p begins to fill, configuration is 1s^2 2s^2 2p^1.
Z = 6, C. A second electron goes into the 2p subshell, but into one of the remaining empty p orbitals (Hund’s rule), with a spin parallel to the first 2p electron. 1s^2 2s^2 2p^2
Z = 7, N. 1s^2 2s^2 2p^3
**Z = 8, O. 1s^2 2s^2 2p^4
Z = 9, F. 1s^2 2s^2 2p^5
Z = 10, Ne. 1s^2 2s^2 2p^6
Z = 11, Na. Represent the Ne configuration as the neon core, [\ce{Ne}], and the one electron remains is a Valence Electron. [\ce{Ne}] 3s^1
Z = 12, Mg. For the other third period elements, only the valence shell electron configurations are shown. 3s^2
Z = 13, Al. 3s^2 3p^1
Z = 14, Si. 3s^2 3p^2 and so forth.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/08 Electrons in Atoms/Electron Spin.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.title: Electron Spin
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.content:
Definition
The electron spin is a Quantum number, m_s, may have a value of + \frac{1}{2}, also denoted by \uparrow, or - \frac{1}{2}, also denoted by \downarrow. The value of m_s does not depend on any of the other three quantum numbers.
Few key details:

An Electron, because of its spin, generates a magnetic field.
A pair of electrons with opposing spins has no net magnetic field.
A silver Atom in its lowest Energy state has only one unpaired electron. The direction of the net magnetic field depends on the spin of the unpaired electron.
In a beam of a large number of silver atoms there is an equal chance that the unpaired electron will have a positive or negative spin.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/08 Electrons in Atoms/Energy Level.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.title: Energy Level
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.content:
Definition
Energy levels are specific, discrete, and Quantized amounts of Energy that bound Systems, such as Electrons in an Atom, are allowed to possess. Electrons occupy fixed Shells at increasing distances from the Nucleus, with higher levels holding more energy.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/08 Electrons in Atoms/Excited State.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.title: Excited State
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.content:
Definition
When a System, usually Atom or a Molecule gains a Quantum of Energy, it moves from the Ground State to a higher level, an excited state.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/08 Electrons in Atoms/Frequency.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.title: Frequency
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.content:
Definition
Frequency is a feature of a Wave, denoted as \nu, is the number of crests that pass through a given point per unit of Time. This means the number of cycles per second. The SI Units for frequency is hertz.\frac{1}{s} = Hz

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/08 Electrons in Atoms/Ground State.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.title: Ground State
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.content:
Definition
The ground state is the lowest Energy, most stable stationary state of a System, such as an Atom or a Molecule.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/08 Electrons in Atoms/Heisenberg Uncertainty Principle.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.title: Heisenberg Uncertainty Principle
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.content:
Definition
The Heisenberg uncertainty principle implies that for a very precise measurement of position, x, many values of Momentum, p, are possible. One way to rationalize this result is to conceive of a highly localized particle as a superposition of many Matter Waves of different de Broglie Wavelengths. The superposition of many waves of different wavelengths produces an interference pattern, which tends to localize the resultant wave, and the particle it describes, to a region of space.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/08 Electrons in Atoms/Orbital Diagram.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.title: Orbital Diagram
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.content:
Definition
An orbital diagram represents the Electron Configuration of an Atom using boxes and arrows to show the Energy, distribution and Electron Spin within Subshells (s,p,d,f).

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/08 Electrons in Atoms/Photoelectric Effect.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.title: Photoelectric Effect
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.content:
Definition
In 1888 Heinrich Hertz discovered that when light strikes the surface of certain Metals, Electrons are ejected. This phenomenon is called the photoelectric effect and the electrons emitted are called photoelectrons. The electron emission only occurs when the Frequency of the incident light is greater than a threshold value \nu _0. When this condition is met:

The number of electrons emitted depends on the intensity of the incident of light.
The Kinetic Energy of the emitted electrons depends on the frequency on the light.
Einstein proposed that electromagnetic radiation has particle like qualities, and they are called Photons.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/08 Electrons in Atoms/Photon.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.title: Photon
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.content:
Definition
A photon is a particle without Mass or Charge that acts as the Quantum of Electromagnetic Radiation, including light and radio Waves. Photons have a characteristic Energy: E_{photon} = h \nu

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/08 Electrons in Atoms/Planck's Constant.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.title: Planck's Constant
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.content:
Definition
Max Planck figured out that Energy is discontinuous, and comes in small packets, Plank’s constant h, with the value:
h = 6.626 \times 10^{-34} Js
The Energy of a quantum of Electromagnetic Radiation is proportional to the Frequency of the radiation, and that is Planck’s equation:
E = h \nu

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/08 Electrons in Atoms/Principal Electronic Shell.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.title: Principal Electronic Shell
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.content:
Definition
All Atomic Orbitals with the same value of n are in the same principal electronic shell. Principals electronic shells are numbered according to the value of n. The value of n related to the Energy and most probable distance of an Electron from the Nucleus.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/08 Electrons in Atoms/Quantum.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.title: Quantum
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.content:
Definition
