The difference between any two allowed Energies of a System has a specific value, called a quantum.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/08 Electrons in Atoms/Schrodinger Equation.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.title: Schrodinger Equation
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.content:
Definition
The Schrodinger equation is a fundamental Partial Differential Equation in Quantum mechanics that describes how the Wave Function of a physical System changes over Time. It acts as the quantum equivalent of Newton’s Second Law, predicting the probability of events rather that definite positions.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/08 Electrons in Atoms/Speed of Light.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.title: Speed of Light
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.content:
Definition
The speed of light is a constant in a vacuum, denoted as c = 2.99 \times 10^8 \frac{m}{s}

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/08 Electrons in Atoms/Standing Wave.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.title: Standing Wave
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.content:
Definition
A standing wave is a Wave pattern that appears to stay in one place, formed by the interference of 2 waves of the same Frequency and Amplitude traveling in opposite directions. They consist of fixed points of no Displacement, known as Nodes and areas of maximum Amplitude, known as Antinodes.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/08 Electrons in Atoms/Subshell.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.title: Subshell
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.content:
Definition
All Atomic Orbitals with the same n and \ell values are in the same subshell. The number of subshells in a Principal Electronic Shell is the same as the number of allowed values of \ell. For example, in the first principal shell, with n = 1, the only allowed value of \ell is 0, and there is a single subshell. The name given to a subshell, regardless of the principal shell in which it is found, depends on the value of \ell. The first 4 subshells are:

s subshell \ell = 0
p subshell \ell = 1
d subshell \ell = 2
f subshell \ell = 3
The number of orbitals in a subshell is the same number of allowed values of m_{\ell} for the particular value of \ell.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/08 Electrons in Atoms/Valence Electron.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.title: Valence Electron
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.content:
Definition
Electrons that are added to the Principal Electronic Shell of the highest principal Quantum number are called valence electrons.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/08 Electrons in Atoms/Wave Function.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.title: Wave Function
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.content:
Definition
A wave function, designated by \Psi(r,t) is a mathematical description of the Quantum state of a particle or System, varying with position and Time. It acts as a probability Amplitude, the square of its magnitude (|\Psi |^2) determines the likelihood of finding a particle in a specific location. It is not a physical Wave but a “cloud of possibilities” that describes how a particle moves before measurement.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/08 Electrons in Atoms/Wave-Particle Duality.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.title: Wave-Particle Duality
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.content:
Definition
Wave-particle duality is the principle that every particle or quantum entity (like Photons or Electrons) behaves as both a Wave and a particle depending on the experimental setup. Light propagates as a wave but interacts as a particle (Photoelectric Effect). Conversely, Matter behaves as particles but can exhibit wave-like Diffraction patterns.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/08 Electrons in Atoms/Wave.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.title: Wave
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.content:
Definition
A wave is a disturbance that transmits Energy through space or a material medium.
The product of the Wavelength and the Frequency of a wave shows how far the wave front travels in a unit of time. This is the speed of the wave.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/08 Electrons in Atoms/Wavelength.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.title: Wavelength
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.content:
Definition
The distance between the tops of two crests of a Wave is called the wavelength, denoted as \lambda.
The product of the wavelength and the Frequency of a wave is the Speed of Light.
c = \nu \lambda

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/08 Electrons in Atoms/Zero Point Energy.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.title: Zero Point Energy
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/08-Electrons.content:
Definition
Zero point energy is the lowest possible Energy that a Quantum physical System may possess, retaining vibrational motion even at absolute zero Temperature.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/09-Periodic-.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/09 Periodic Trends/09 Periodic Trends.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/09-Periodic-.title: 09 Periodic Trends
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/09-Periodic-.content:
Overview
The experimental basis of the Periodic Table of the Elements is the Periodic Law: Certain Properties recure periodically when the elements are arranged by increasing Atomic Number. The theoretical basis is that the properties of an element are related to the Electron Configuration of its Atoms, and elements in the same Group of the periodic table have similar electron configurations.
The 3 classes of elements in the periodic table are the Nonmetals, Metals, and Metalloids. Metalloids have some properties characteristic of metals and some of nonmetals. The nonmetals are further divided into the Noble Gases and the remainder of the main-group nonmetals, while metals include the main-group metals and transition elements.
The types of Atomic Radii include Covalent Radii, Metallic Radii, and Van Der Waals Radii. In general, atomic radii decreases across a Period and increase down a group of the periodic table, mirroring the variation in Effective Nuclear Charge, across a period and down a group. The Ionic Radii of positive Ions are smaller than the neutral atom, whereas negative ions are larger than the parent atom. Ionic radii exhibit adherence to the periodic law similar to that of atomic radii. When atoms or ions have the same number of Electrons, they are said to be Isoelectronic. When the radii of isoelectronic species are compared, the more negative the Charge, the larger the radius of the ion or atom.
A study of Ionization Energy, E_i , shows that the periodic relationship observed is governed by the variation of Z_{\text{eff}}.
Electron Affinity, E_{ea} , is the Energy change when an electron is added to a gaseous atom. Interpreting trends is somewhat more difficult for electron affinity than for ionization energy because of the additional electron repulsions that arise when an electron is added to an atom.
The magnetic properties of an atom or ion stem from the presence or absence of unpaired electrons. Paramagnetic atoms and ions have one or more unpaired electrons. In Diamagnetic atoms and ions, all electrons are paired.
The Polarizability of an atom provides a measure of the extent to which its electron cloud can be distorted by an Electric Field or the approach of another atom, Molecule or ion. Polarizability increases as the size of the atom increases.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/09-Periodic-.title: Atomic Radius
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/09-Periodic-.content:
Definition
The atomic radius measures the size of an Atom, as half the distance between the Nuclei of two bonded atoms. It decreases across a period and increases down a Group, due to added Shells.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/09-Periodic-.title: Covalent Radius
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/09-Periodic-.content:
Definition
The covalent radius is one half the distance between the Nuclei of 2 identical Atoms joined by a single Covalent Bond.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/09-Periodic-.title: Diamagnetic
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/09-Periodic-.content:
Definition
In a diamagnetic Atom or Ion, all Electrons are paired and the individual magnetic effects cancel out. A diamagnetic species is weakly repelled by Magnetic Fields.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/09-Periodic-.title: Electron Affinity
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/09-Periodic-.content:
Definition
Electron affinity, E_{ea} can be defined as the Enthalpy change, \Delta _{ea} H, that occurs when an Atom in the Gas phase gains an Electron. It reflects the Energy change in the process.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/09-Periodic-.title: Groups
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/09-Periodic-.content:
Definition
A group is a column of Elements in the Periodic Table. There are 18 numbered groups in the periodic table. The elements in a group have similar Physical Properties or Chemical Properties of the outermost Electron Shells of their Atoms.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/09-Periodic-.title: Ionic Radius
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/09-Periodic-.content:
Definition
The ionic radius is based on the distance between the Nuclei of Ions joined by an Ionic Bond.
The nucleus draws the Electrons in closer, so Cations are smaller than the atoms from which they are formed, and Anions are bigger.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/09-Periodic-.title: Ionization Energy
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/09-Periodic-.content:
Definition
The ionization energy, E_i is the quantity of Energy an Atom must absorb to be able to expel an Electron. With relatively few exceptions, Ionization energies increase from left to right across a period and decrease from top to bottom within a Group. Ionization energies decrease as Atomic Radius increase.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/09-Periodic-.title: Isoelectronicity
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/09-Periodic-.content:
Definition
Isoelectronic species are Atoms, Ions or Molecules that share the same number of Electrons and the same Ground State Electron Configuration. They differ in Atomic Number and Charge. Generally, across an isoelectronic species, increasing charge decreases Ionic Radius.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/09-Periodic-.title: Metal
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/09-Periodic-.content:
Definition
A metal is an Element that is usually Solid at room Temperature (except Mercury). Metals can conduct Heat and electricity. They are malleable (can be flattened into thin sheets), ductile (can be drawn into wires), and have a lustrous and shiny appearance.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/09-Periodic-.title: Metallic Radius
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/09-Periodic-.content:
Definition
A metallic radius is one half the distance between the Nuclei of 2 Atoms in contact in the crystalline Solid Metal.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/09-Periodic-.title: Metalloid
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/09-Periodic-.content:
Definition
A metalloid is an Element that looks like a Metal and in some ways behaves like metals but also has some Nonmetal like Properties.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/09-Periodic-.title: Noble Gas
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/09-Periodic-.content:
Definition
The noble gases are Elements that are members of Group 18 of the Periodic Table. Under standard conditions, They are odorless, colorless, have a full outer valence Shell making them non reactive.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/09-Periodic-.title: Nonmetal
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/09-Periodic-.content:
Definition
A nonmetal is an Element that has the opposite Properties of a Metal. Nonmetals are poor conductors of Heat and electricity, they can be a Gas in room Temperature, some can be brittle Solids.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/09-Periodic-.title: Paramagnetic
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/09-Periodic-.content:
Definition
A paramagnetic Atom or Ion has unpaired Electrons, and the individual magnetic effects do not cancel out. The unpaired electrons possess a magnetic Moment that causes the atom or ion to be attracted to an external Magnetic Field. The more unpaired electrons present, the stronger is this attraction.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/09-Periodic-.title: Periodic Law
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/09-Periodic-.content:
Definition
The periodic law states that the Physical Properties and Chemical Properties of Elements are periodic functions of their Atomic Numbers. When elements are arranged in order of increasing number, similar Properties recure periodically.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/09-Periodic-.title: Periodic Table
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/09-Periodic-.content:
Definition
The periodic table organizes Elements into 18 vertical Groups and 7 horizontal Periods. Elements in the same group have similar Chemical Properties and the same number of Valence Electrons. Elements in the same period have the same number of Electron Shells, with Properties changing gradually from left to right.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/09-Periodic-.title: Periods
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/09-Periodic-.content:
Definition
A period on the Periodic Table is a row of Elements. All elements in a row have the same number of Electron Shells. Each next element in a period has one or more Proton and is less Metallic than its predecessor. Arranged this way, elements in the same Group have similar Chemical Properties and Physical Properties, reflecting the Periodic Law.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/09-Periodic-.title: Polarizability
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/09-Periodic-.content:
Definition
The polarizability of an Atom measures the extent to which its Electron cloud can be distorted. Polarizability increases with the size of the atom. It is similar in magnitude to the atomic Volume calculated from the Atomic Radius.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/09-Periodic-.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/09 Periodic Trends/Van Der Waals Radius.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/09-Periodic-.title: Van Der Waals Radius
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/09-Periodic-.content:
Definition
A van der Waals radius is defined as the distance between the centers of neighboring Atoms in a Solid sample of a Noble Gas.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/10-Bonding-I.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/10 Bonding I/10 Bonding I.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/10-Bonding-I.title: 10 Bonding I
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/10-Bonding-I.content:
Overview
A Lewis Symbol represents the Valence Electrons of an Atom by using dots placed around the chemical symbol. A Lewis Structure is a combination of Lewis symbols used to represent Chemical Bonds. Normally, all the Electrons in a Lewis structure are paired, and each atom in the structure acquires an Octet, that is, there are 8 electrons as valence electrons. In Lewis Theory, chemical bonds are classified as Ionic Bonds, which are formed by electron transfer between atoms, or Covalent Bond, which are formed by electrons shared between atoms. Most bonds, however, have partial ionic and partial covalent characteristics.
Atoms in Molecules are often surrounded by 8 valence electrons and thus conform to the octet rule. In covalent bonds, pairs of electrons shared between 2 atoms to form the bonds are called Bond Pairs, whereas pairs of electrons not shared in chemical bond are called Lone Pairs. A single pair of electrons shared between 2 atoms constitutes a Single Covalent Bond. When both electrons in a covalent bond between 2 atoms are provided by only one of the atoms, the bond is called a coordinate covalent bond. To construct a Lewis structure for a molecule in which all atoms obey the octet rule, it is often necessary for atoms to share more than one pair of electrons, thus forming multiple covalent bonds. 2 shared electron pairs constitutes a Double Covalent Bond and 3 shared pairs a Triple Covalent Bond.
A covalent bond in which the electron pair is not shared equally by the bonded atoms is called a Polar Covalent Bond. Whether a bond is polar or not can be predicted by comparing the Electronegativity of the atoms involved. The greater the Electronegativity Difference between 2 atoms in a chemical bond, the more polar the bond and the more ionic its character. The electron Charge distribution in a molecule can be visualized by computing an electrostatic potential map.
To draw the Lewis structure of a covalent molecule, one needs to know the Skeletal Structure, that is, which is the Central Atom and what atoms are bonded to it. Atoms that are bonded to just one other atoms are called Terminal Atoms. Typically, the atom with the lowest electronegativity is a central atom. At times, the concept of Formal Charge is useful in selecting a skeletal structure and assessing the plausibility of a Lewis structure.
Often, more than one plausible Lewis structure can be written for a species. This situation is called Resonance. In these cases the true structure is a resonance hybrid of 2 or more contributing structures.
There are often exceptions to the octet rule.

Odd-electron species, such as \ce{NO}, have an unpaired electron and are Paramagnetic. Many of these species are reactive molecular fragments, such as \ce{OH}, called Free Radicals.
A few molecules have incomplete octets in their Lewis structures, that is, not enough electrons to provide an octet for every atom.
Expanded Valence Shells occur in some Compounds of Nonmetals of the 3rd Period and beyond.
In these, the valence shell of the central atom must be expanded to 10 or 12 electrons in order to write a Lewis structure.

A powerful method for predicting the Molecular Geometry, or molecule shape, of a species is the valence shell electron pair repulsion theory or the VSEPR Theory. The shape of a molecule or a polyatomic ion depends on the geometric distribution of valence shell electron Groups- the Electron-Group Geometry, and whether these groups contain bonding electrons or lone pairs. The angles between the electron groups provide a method for predicting Bond Angles in a molecule. An important use of information about the shapes of molecules is in establishing whether bonds in a molecule combine to produce a Dipole Moment. Molecules with a resultant dipole moment are Polar Molecules, those with no resultant dipole moment are nonpolar.
Single, double, and triple covalent bonds are said to have a Bond Order of 1, 2, and 3, respectively. Bond Length is the distance between the centers of 2 atoms joined by a covalent bond. The greater the bond order, the shorter the bond length.
Bond Dissociation Energy, D, is the quantity of Energy required to break one Mole of Covalent Bonds in a gaseous molecule. Average Bond Energies can be used to estimate Enthalpy changes for Reactions involving Gases.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/10-Bonding-I.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/10 Bonding I/Average Bond Energy.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/10-Bonding-I.title: Average Bond Energy
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/10-Bonding-I.content:
Definition
An average bond energy is the average of Bond Dissociation Energies for a number of different species. Double Covalent Bond have higher bond energies than Single Covalent Bond between the same Atoms but they are not twice as large. Triple Covalent Bond are the strongest.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/10-Bonding-I.title: Bond Angle
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/10-Bonding-I.content:
Definition
The bond angles, the angles between adjacent lines representing a Chemical Bond.

A diatomic Molecule has only one bond and no bond angle. Because the geometric shape determined by 2 points is a straight line, all diatomic molecules are linear.
A triatomic molecule has two bonds and one bond angle. If the bond angle is 180 \degree, the 3 Atoms lie on a straight line, and the molecule is linear. For any other bond angle, a triatomic molecule has a V-shape.
Some polyatomic molecules with more than 3 atoms have a planer or even linear shapes. More commonly, the centers of the atoms in these molecules define a 3D geometric figure.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/10-Bonding-I.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/10 Bonding I/Bond Dissociation Energy.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/10-Bonding-I.title: Bond Dissociation Energy
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/10-Bonding-I.content:
Definition
**Bond dissociation energy, ** D is the quantity of Energy required to break one Mole of Covalent Bonds in a species. We can think of bond dissociation energy as an Enthalpy change or a Heat of Reaction.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/10-Bonding-I.title: Bond Length
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/10-Bonding-I.content:
Definition
The bond length is the distance between the center of 2 Atoms joined by a Covalent Bond. A Double Covalent Bond is shorter than a Single Covalent Bond, and Triple Covalent Bond is the shortest. The Length of the covalent bond between 2 atoms can be approximated as the sum of the Covalent Radii of the two atoms.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/10-Bonding-I.title: Bond Order
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/10-Bonding-I.content:
Definition
The bond order describes whether a Covalent Bond is Single Covalent Bond (bond order = 1), Double Covalent Bond (bond order = 2), or Triple Covalent Bond (bond order = 3). The more Electrons present, the more tightly the Atoms are held together.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/10-Bonding-I.title: Bond Pair
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/10-Bonding-I.content:
Definition
In the Lewis Theory, bond pair refers to a pair of Electrons in a Covalent Bond. It is customary to replace bond pairs with lines (\ce{A - B})

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/10-Bonding-I.title: Central Atom
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/10-Bonding-I.content:
Definition
A central atom is Bonded to 2 or more Atoms in the Skeletal Structure. Central atoms are generally those with the lowest Electronegativity. Carbon atoms are always central atoms.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/10-Bonding-I.title: Chemical Bond
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/10-Bonding-I.content:
Definition
A chemical bond is a lasting electrostatic attraction that holds Atoms or Ions together, allowing them to form stable Compounds by sharing or transferring Valence Electrons. There are a few types of bonds: Covalent Bond, Ionic Bond, Metallic Bond.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/10-Bonding-I.title: Chemical Resonance
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/10-Bonding-I.content:
Definition
The situation in which 2 or more plausible Lewis Structures contribute to the correct structure is called resonance. The true structure is a resonance hybrid of plausible contributing structures. Acceptable contributing structures to a resonance hybrid must all have equal Skeletal Structure, they can differ only in how Electrons are distributed withing the structure. The two contributing structures are joined by a double headed arrow. We can decide which resonance structure likely contributes most to the hybrid by applying the general rules for Formal Charge.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/10-Bonding-I.title: Covalent Bond
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/10-Bonding-I.content:
Definition
A covalent bond is a type of Chemical Bond in which Atoms share pairs of Valence Electrons, typically between Nonmetals. These bonds can be

Single Covalent Bond
Double Covalent Bond
Triple Covalent Bond

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/10-Bonding-I.title: Dipole Moment
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/10-Bonding-I.content:
Definition
The extent of the Charge Displacement in a Polar Covalent Bond is given by the dipole moment, \mu. The dipole moment is the product of a partial charge (\delta) and distance (d).
\mu = \delta \times d

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/10-Bonding-I.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/10 Bonding I/Double Covalent Bond.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/10-Bonding-I.title: Double Covalent Bond
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/10-Bonding-I.content:
Definition
In Lewis Structure, the bounded Atoms are seen to share 2 Bond Pair of Electrons between them is a double covalent bond (\ce{A = B}).

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/10-Bonding-I.title: Electron-Group Geometry
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/10-Bonding-I.content:
Definition
Electron-group geometry describes the spatial arrangement of all Electron groups (Bond Pairs and Lone Pairs) around a Central Atom to minimize repulsion. Based on VSEPR Theory, these geometries determine the basic shape of a Molecule.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/10-Bonding-I.title: Electronegativity Difference
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/10-Bonding-I.content:
Definition
The Absolute Value of the difference in Electronegativity values of the bonded Atoms is called the electronegativity difference, \Delta EN. If \Delta EN for two atoms is very small, the bond between them is a Covalent Bond. If \Delta EN is large, the bond is an Ionic Bond. For intermediate values of \Delta EN the bond is described as Polar Covalent Bond.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/10-Bonding-I.title: Electronegativity
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/10-Bonding-I.content:
Definition
Electronegativity, \Delta EN, describes an Atom’s ability to compete for Electrons with other atoms to which it is bonded. Electronegativity is related to Ionization Energy and Electron Affinity.
EN_A \propto E_i(A)-E_{ea}(A)
An Element with a high ionization energy and electron affinity that is large and negative, will have a large electronegativity.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/10-Bonding-I.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/10 Bonding I/Expanded Valence Shell.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/10-Bonding-I.title: Expanded Valence Shell
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/10-Bonding-I.content:
Definition
There are a few Lewis Structure that stand out by having 10 or 12 Valence Electrons around the Central Atom, creating an expanded valence shell. Molecules with expanded valence shells typically involve Nonmetal Atoms of the third period and beyond that are in a Chemical Bond with highly Electronegativity atoms.
By assuming that after the 3s and 3p Subshells of the Central Atom fill to capacity (8 electrons), extra electrons go into the empty 3d subshell.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/10-Bonding-I.title: Formal Charge
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/10-Bonding-I.content:
Definition
Formal charge (\ce{FC}) are apparent Charges on certain Atoms in a Lewis Structure that arise when atoms have not contributed equal numbers of Electrons to the Covalent Bond sharing them.
The formal charge on an atom in a Lewis structure is the number of Valence Electron in the free atom minus the number of electrons assigned to that atom in the Lewis structure:

Count Lone Pair electrons as belonging to the atom on which they are found.
Divide Bond Pair electrons equally between the Bonded atoms.


General Rules of Lewis Structure Based on Its Formal Charge

The sum of the formal charges in a Lewis structure must be 0 for a neutral Molecule and must equal the magnitude of the charge for a polyatomic Ion.
Where formal charges are required, they should be as small as possible.
Negative formal charges usually appear on the most Electronegative atoms, positive charges on the least electronegative atoms.
Structure having formal charges of the same sign on adjacent atoms are unlikely.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/10-Bonding-I.title: Free Radical
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/10-Bonding-I.content:
Definition
The free radicals are highly reactive molecular fragments with one or more unpaired Electrons. The Chemical Formula of free radicals are usually written with a dot to emphasize the presence of an unpaired electron.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/10-Bonding-I.title: Ionic Bond
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/10-Bonding-I.content:
Definition
An ionic bond is a type of Chemical Bond in which occurs a complete transfer of Electrons, usually between a Metal and a Nonmetal, creating positively and negatively Charged Ions that attract.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/10-Bonding-I.title: Lewis Structure
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/10-Bonding-I.content:
Definition
A Lewis structure is a combination of Lewis Symbols that represents either the transfer or the sharing of Electrons in a Chemical Bond.

A Strategy for Writing Lewis Structures

Determine the total number of Valence Electrons that must appear in the structure.
Identify the Central Atom(s) and Terminal Atoms.
Write a plausible Skeletal Structure. Join the Atoms by Single Covalent Bonds.
For each bond in the skeletal structure, subtract 2 from the total number of valence electrons.
With the valence electrons remaining, first complete the Octets of the terminal atoms. Then complete the octets of the central atoms. If there are just enough valence electrons to complete octets for all the atoms, the structure is complete.
If one or more central atoms are left with an incomplete octet, move Lone Pair electrons from one or more terminal atoms to form Double Covalent Bond or Triple Covalent Bond to central atoms.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/10-Bonding-I.title: Lewis Symbol
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/10-Bonding-I.content:
Definition
Lewis developed a set of symbols for his Theory. A Lewis symbol consists of a chemical symbol to represent the Nucleus and core Electrons (inner Shell), together with dots placed around the symbol to represent the Valence Electron. The Lewis symbol for silicon is
\begin{array}{c}
\cdot \\
\cdot \; \mathrm{Si} \; \cdot \\
\cdot
\end{array}$$

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/10-Bonding-I.title: Lewis Theory
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/10-Bonding-I.content:
Definition
The Lewis theory explains Chemical Bond and Acid Base behavior through the transfer or sharing of Electron pairs to achieve stable Noble Gas Configuration. Some fundamental ideas associated with the Lewis theory follow:

Electrons, especially Valence Electrons, play a fundamental role in chemical bonding.
In some cases, electrons are transferred from one Atom to another. Positive and negative Ions are formed and attract each other through electrostatic Forces called Ionic Bonds.
In other cases one or more pairs of electrons are shared between atoms, a Covalent Bond.
Electrons are transferred or shared in such a way that each atom acquires an especially stable electron configuration, an Octet.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/10-Bonding-I.title: Lone Pair
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/10-Bonding-I.content:
Definition
In the Lewis Theory, a lone pair refers to a pair of Electrons that are not involved in a Chemical Bond.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/10-Bonding-I.title: Metallic Bond
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/10-Bonding-I.content:
Definition
A metallic bond a type of Chemical Bond between positive Metal Ions and a surrounding “sea” of delocalized, freely moving outer Electrons

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/10-Bonding-I.title: Molecular Geometry
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/10-Bonding-I.content:
Definition
Molecular geometry is the 3-dimensional arrangement of Atoms within a Molecule, determined by Bond Lengths, Bond Angles and Lone Pair repulsion. Based on the VSEPR Theory, Electron pairs surrounding a Central Atom arrange themselves to minimize repulsion, directly impacting a Substance reactivity, Polarity and Physical Properties.
Key molecular shapes:

Linear: 2 electron domains, 180 angle.
Trigonal Planar: 3 electron domains, 120 angle.
Tetrahedral: 4 electron domains, 109.5 angle.
Trigonal Bipyramidal: 5 electron domains, 90 and 120 angles.
Octahedral: 6 electron domains, 90 angle.

Lone pairs occupy more space than Bond Pairs, forcing Bonds closer together and reducing bond angles.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/10-Bonding-I.title: Octet
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/10-Bonding-I.content:
Definition
The octet rule is a chemical rule of thumb that reflects the theory that main Group Elements tend to create a Chemical Bond in such a way that each Atom has 8 Electrons as Valence Electrons, giving it the same Electron Configuration as a Noble Gas.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/10-Bonding-I.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/10 Bonding I/Polar Covalent Bond.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/10-Bonding-I.title: Polar Covalent Bond
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/10-Bonding-I.content:
Definition
A Covalent Bond in which Electrons are not shared equally between two Atoms is called a polar covalent bond.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/10-Bonding-I.title: Polar Molecule
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/10-Bonding-I.content:
Definition
A polar molecule is a Molecule with a Covalent Bond with an unequal distribution of Charges, resulting in a positive end and a negative end. We use a cross base arrow (-|\rightarrow)

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/10-Bonding-I.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/10 Bonding I/Single Covalent Bond.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/10-Bonding-I.title: Single Covalent Bond
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/10-Bonding-I.content:
Definition
The sharing of a single Bond Pair of Electrons between bounded Atoms produces a single covalent bond. This is a type of Chemical Bond.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/10-Bonding-I.title: Skeletal Structure
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/10-Bonding-I.content:
Definition
The starting point in writing a Lewis Structure is to designate the skeletal structure, all the Atoms in the structure arranged in the order in which they are Bonded to one another. In a skeletal structure with more than 2 atoms, we need to distinguish between Central and Terminal Atoms.
Transclude of Skeletal-Structure.excalidraw

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/10-Bonding-I.title: Terminal Atom
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/10-Bonding-I.content:
Definition
A terminal atom is Bonded to just one other Atom in a Skeletal Structure. Hydrogen atoms are always terminal atoms, because an \ce{H} atom can accommodate only 2 Valence Electrons, it can form only one Chemical Bond to another atom.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/10-Bonding-I.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/10 Bonding I/Triple Covalent Bond.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/10-Bonding-I.title: Triple Covalent Bond
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/10-Bonding-I.content:
Definition
A triple covalent bond is a type of Chemical Bond where 2 Atoms share 3 Bond Pair, (\ce{A \equiv B}).

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/10-Bonding-I.title: VSEPR Theory
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/10-Bonding-I.content:
Definition
The valence shell electron pair repulsion theory (VSEPR theory) is meant to understand the arrangement of Valence Electrons in the valence Shell of a Central Atom in a Lewis Structure. Another aspect of VSEPR theory is a focus not just on Electron pairs but on electrons groups. A group of electrons can be a Lone Pair, Bond Pair or a single unpaired electron on an Atom with an incomplete Octet.
We can represent a 3D shape of a Molecule:

Ordinary lines are used to represent Bonds that lie in the plane of the paper.
Solid wedges are used to represent bonds that point outward of the paper.
Dashed wedges are used to represent bonds that point inward of the paper.


Applying VSEPR Theory

Draw a plausible Lewis structure of the species.
Determine the number of electron groups around the central atom, and identify them as being bond pair electron groups or lone pairs of electrons.
Establish the electron group geometry around the central atom—linear, triagonal planer, tetrahedral, triagonal bipyramidal, or octahedral.
Determine the molecular geometry from the position of the atoms bonded directly to the central atom.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/11-Bonding-I.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/11 Bonding II/11 Bonding II.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/11-Bonding-I.title: 11 Bonding II
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/11-Bonding-I.content:
Overview
A basic requirement of a bonding theory is that it provide a better description of the electronic structure of Molecules than the simple ideas of the Lewis Theory. The transfer of Electron Density from regions outside the Nuclei to regions nearer and between the nuclei produces a significant decrease in the Potential Energy of the electrons and contributes substantially to the stability of a Chemical Bond.
Valence Bond Method considers a Covalent Bond in terms of the overlap of Atomic Orbitals of the bonded atoms.
Some molecules can be described in terms of the overlap if simple orbitals, but often orbitals that are composite of simple orbitals, Hybrid Orbitals, are needed. The Hybridization scheme chosen is the one that produces an orientation of hybrid orbitals to match the Electron-Group Geometry predicted by the VSEPR Theory. sp hybrid orbitals are associated with linear electron group geometries. sp^2 hybrid orbitals with trigonal planer geometries, sp^3 hybrid orbitals with tetrahedral geometries, sp^3d hybrid orbitals with trigonal bipyramidal geometries and sp^3d^2 hybrid orbitals with octahedral geometries.
End to end overlap of orbitals produces Sigma Bonds. Side to side overlap of 2 p orbitals produces a Pi Bond. Single Covalent Bond are sigma bonds. A Double Covalent Bond consists of one sigma bond and one pi bond. A Triple Covalent Bond consists of one sigma bond and 2 pi bonds. The geometric shape of a species determines the sigma bond framework, and pi bonds are added as required to complete the bonding description.
In Molecular Orbital Theory, electrons are assigned to molecular orbitals. The numbers and kinds of molecular orbitals are related to the atomic orbitals used to generate them. Electron density between Atoms is high in Bonding Molecular Orbitals and very low in Antibonding Orbitals. Bond Order is one half the difference between the numbers of electrons in bonding molecular orbitals and in antibonding molecular orbitals. Molecular orbital Energy Level diagrams and an Aufbau process can be used to describe the electronic structure of a molecule.
Bonding in the benzene molecule, \ce{C6H6} , is partially based on the concept of Delocalized Molecular Orbitals. These are regions of high electron density that extend over several atoms in a molecule. Delocalized molecular orbitals also provide an alternative to the concept of Resonance in other molecules and Ions.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/11-Bonding-I.title: Antibonding Orbitals
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/11-Bonding-I.content:
Definition
An antibonding orbital is a tape of Molecular Orbital that, when occupied by Electrons, decreases the stability of a Molecule and oppose the Chemical Bond formation. Formed by destructive interference of Atomic Orbitals, these high Energy orbitals have a Node between Nuclei, causing increased repulsion.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/11-Bonding-I.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/11 Bonding II/Bonding Molecular Orbitals.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/11-Bonding-I.title: Bonding Molecular Orbitals
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/11-Bonding-I.content:
Definition
A bonding molecular orbital is a region of high Electron probability created by the constructive, in-phase overlap of Atomic Orbitals. These orbitals are lower in Energy than the original atomic orbitals, stabilizing the Molecule by concentrating electron density between Nuclei, resulting in attraction rather than repulsion.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/11-Bonding-I.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/11 Bonding II/Delocalized Molecular Orbitals.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/11-Bonding-I.title: Delocalized Molecular Orbitals
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/11-Bonding-I.content:
Definition
Delocalized molecular orbitals are Quantum Wavefunctions that extend over several Atoms or the entire Molecule, rather than being confined to a single Bond or atom. They arise from the Linear Combination of Atomic Orbitals in Conjugated Systems and are essential for describing aromatic compounds, Resonance, and bonding in Metals.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/11-Bonding-I.title: Hybrid Orbital
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/11-Bonding-I.content:
Definition
The new Atomic Orbital that forms with Hybridization is called an hybrid orbital.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/11-Bonding-I.title: Hybridization
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/11-Bonding-I.content:
Definition
The mathematical process of transforming pure Atomic Orbitals into reformulated atomic orbitals for Bonded Atoms is called hybridization.
some useful points:

For a given hybridization scheme, the number of Hybrid Orbitals equals the total number of atomic orbitals that are combined.
The objective of a hybridization scheme is an after the fact rationalization of the experimentally observed shape of a Molecule. Its not an actual physical phenomenon.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/11-Bonding-I.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/11 Bonding II/Molecular Orbital Theory.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/11-Bonding-I.title: Molecular Orbital Theory
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/11-Bonding-I.content:
Definition
The molecular orbit theory describes Chemical Bond by assuming Atomic Orbitals combine to form new delocalized molecular orbitals spread across the entire Molecule. Each molecular orbital can be represented as a Linear Combination of atomic orbitals. The total number of molecular orbitals is equal to the total number of atomic orbitals. They can be classified as bonding antibonding or nonbonding. The Electron Configuration for the molecule is obtained by placing the Electrons into the molecular orbitals in a particular order.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/11-Bonding-I.title: Pi Bond
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/11-Bonding-I.content:
Definition
A pi bond is a type of Covalent Bond formed by the side to side overlap of 2 Atomic Orbitals on adjacent Atoms. These bonds feature electron density concentrated in 2 lobes, one above and one below the internuclear axis, and are weaker than Sigma Bonds.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/11-Bonding-I.title: Sigma Bond
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/11-Bonding-I.content:
Definition
A sigma bond is the strongest type of Covalent Bond, formed by the head on overlap of Atomic Orbitals (s,p, or Hybrid Orbital)  along the internuclear axis. The shape of a Molecule is determined only by the orbitals forming sigma bonds.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/11-Bonding-I.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/11 Bonding II/Valence Bond Method.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/11-Bonding-I.title: Valence Bond Method
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/11-Bonding-I.content:
Definition
A description of Covalent Bond formation in terms of Atomic Orbital overlap is called the valence bond method. The valence bon method gives a localized Electron model of bonding: Core electrons and Lone Pair Valence Electrons retain the same orbital location as in the separated Atoms, but the bonding electrons do not. Instead, they are described by an electron probability density that includes the region of orbital overlap and both Nuclei.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/12-Intermole.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/12 Intermolecular Forces/12 Intermolecular Forces.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/12-Intermole.title: 12 Intermolecular Forces
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/12-Intermole.content:
Overview
The intermolecular forces that occur between Molecules are collectively known as Van Der Waals Forces. The most common intermolecular Forces of attraction are those between instantaneous and induced dipoles, the London Forces. The magnitudes of London forces depend on how easily Electron Displacements within molecules cause a temporary imbalance of electron Charge distribution, that is, on the Polarizability of the molecules. In Polar Substances, there are also Dipole Dipole Interactions. Some hydrogen-containing Substances exhibit significant intermolecular attractions called Hydrogen Bonds, in which \ce{H} atoms Bonded to highly Electronegative Atoms- \ce{N},\ce{O},\ce{F} in a molecule are simultaneously attracted to other highly electronegative atoms in the same molecule or in different molecules. Hydrogen bonding has a profound effect on Physical Properties, such as Boiling Point and its a vital intermolecular force in living Systems.
Surface Tension, the Energy required to extend the surface off a Liquid, and Viscosity, a liquid’s resistance to flow, are Properties related to intermolecular forces. Familiar phenomena such as drop shape, meniscus formation, and capillary action depend on surface tension. Specifically, these phenomena are influenced by the balance between Cohesive Forces, intermolecular forces between molecules in a liquid, and Adhesive Force, intermolecular forces between liquid molecules and a surface. Vapor Pressure, the Pressure exerted by a Vapor in Equilibrium with a liquid, is a measure of the volatility of a liquid and is related to the strength of intermolecular forces. The conversion of a liquid to a vapor is called Evaporation. The reverse process is called Condensation. The dependence of vapor pressure on Temperature is represented by a Vapor Pressure Curve and can be expressed in the Clausius Clapeyron Equation. When the pressure exerted by the escaping molecules from the surface of the liquid equals the pressure exerted by the molecules in the atmosphere, Boiling is said to occur. The Normal Boiling Point is the temperature at which the vapor pressure of the liquid equals 1 atm. The Critical Point is the condition of temperature and pressure at which a liquid and its vapor become indistinguishable.
When crystalline Solids are heated, a temperature is reached where the solid state is converted to a liquid, Melting occurs. The temperature at which this occurs is the Melting Point. When liquids are cooled, the crystalline material will form during the process of Freezing, and the temperature at which this occurs is the Freezing Point. Under certain conditions solids can directly convert into vapor by the process of Sublimation. The reverse process is called Deposition. Among the properties of a solid affected by intermolecular forces are its sublimation pressure and its melting point.
A Phase Diagram is a graphical plot of conditions under which solids, liquids and gases (vapors) exist, as single phases or as 2 or more phases in equilibrium with one another. Significant points on a phase diagram are the Triple Point (where all 3 coexist), melting and boiling point and critical point, beyond which a supercritical fluid is possible. Some Substances can exist in different forms in the solid state, such behavior is called Polymorphism.
Solids can be classified according to the nature of bonding. In Network Covalent Solids, Chemical Bonds extend throughout a crystalline structure. For these substances the chemical bonds are the forces holding the atoms in place. Ionic Solids are composed of Ions held in place through interionic forces of attractions. Solids that are composed of discrete molecules are known as Molecular Solids. These molecules are held in place through the different intermolecular forces. Metal Atoms form Metallic Solids through the delocalization of electrons. The delocalized electrons freely move throughout the solid, lending to it various properties, such as Conductivity. Lattice Energy is the energy released when separated gaseous ions come together to form one Mole of an ionic solid.
Some Crystal structures can be described in terms of packing of spheres. Depending on the way in which the spheres are packed, different Unit Cells are obtained. The hexagonal unit cell is obtained with Hexagonal Closest Packed (hcp) spheres. A Face Centered Cubic (fcc) unit cell is obtained with Cubic Closest Packed spheres. A Body Centered Cubic (bcc) unit cell is found in some cases where spheres are not packed as closely as in the hcp and fcc structures. The dimensions of the unit cell can be determined by X-ray diffraction, and these dimensions can be used in calculating Atomic Radius and Density. An important consideration with ionic crystals is that the ions are not all of the same size or charge. Ionic crystals can often be viewed as an array of Anions with the Cations fitting in the holes within the anion array.
Lattice energies of ionic crystals can be related to certain atomic and thermodynamic properties by means of the Born-Fajans-Haber cycle.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/12-Intermole.title: Adhesive Force
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/12-Intermole.content:
Definition
The Force between Liquid Molecules and the surface is called an adhesive force. If adhesive forces are strong enough, the Energy requirement for spreading the liquid drop into a film is met through the Work done by the collapsing drop.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/12-Intermole.title: Boiling Point
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/12-Intermole.content:
Definition
The Temperature at which the Vapor Pressure of a Liquid is equal to STP is the normal boiling point.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/12-Intermole.title: Boiling
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/12-Intermole.content:
Definition
When a Liquid is Heated in a container open to the  atmosphere, there is a particular Temperature at which Evaporation occurs throughout the liquid rather than at the surface. Vapor bubbles form within the bulk of the liquid, rise to the surface and escape. The Pressure exerted by escaping Molecules equals that exerted by molecules of the atmosphere and boiling occurs.
During boiling, Energy absorbed as heat is used only to convert molecules of liquid into vapor. The temperature remains constant until all the liquid has boiled.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/12-Intermole.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/12 Intermolecular Forces/Clausius Clapeyron Equation.md

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/12-Intermole.title: Cohesive Force
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/12-Intermole.content:
Definition
The Force between Molecules holding them together in a drop of a Liquid is called a cohesive force. If cohesive forces are strong compared with Adhesive Forces, a drop maintains its shape.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/12-Intermole.title: Condensation
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/12-Intermole.content:
Definition
The conversion of a Gas or Vapor to a Liquid is called condensation. That is the reverse of Evaporation. Thus,
\Delta _{cond}H = -\Delta _{vap}H
Condensation is an Exothermic Reaction. This explains why burns produced by a given Mass of steam are much more severe than burns produced by the same mass of hot Water.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/12-Intermole.title: Critical Point
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/12-Intermole.content:
Definition
The critical point is the point at which the following conditions are reached and the Liquid and Vapor become indistinguishable.

The Density of the liquid decreases, that of the vapor increases and the two become equal.
The Surface Tension of the liquid approaches zero. The interface between the liquid and vapor becomes less distinct and eventually disappears.
The Temperature at the critical point is the critical temperature, T_c and the Pressure is the critical pressure, P_c. The critical point is the highest point on a Vapor Pressure curve and represents the highest temperature at which the liquid can exist.
A Gas can be liquified only at temperatures below its critical temperature.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/12-Intermole.title: Deposition
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/12-Intermole.content:
Definition
The Reverse Process to Sublimation, the passage of Molecules from the Vapor to the Solid state is called deposition.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/12-Intermole.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/12 Intermolecular Forces/Dipole Dipole Interactions.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/12-Intermole.title: Dipole Dipole Interactions
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/12-Intermole.content:
Definition
Dipole dipole interactions are electrostatic attractions between the partial positive end of one Polar Molecule and the partial negative end of another, resulting from permanent Dipole Moments.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/12-Intermole.title: Dynamic Equilibrium
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/12-Intermole.content:
Definition
Dynamic equilibrium is a state in Reversible Processes where forward and reverse reactions occur at the same rate, resulting in no net chance in the concentration of Reagents and Products

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/12-Intermole.title: Evaporation
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/12-Intermole.content:
Definition
Earlier we saw that the speed and Kinetic Energy of Molecules vary over a wide range at any given Temperature. We also learned that molecules having kinetic energies above the average value are able to overcome Van Der Waals Forces and escape from the surface of the Liquid into the gaseous state. This passage of molecules from the surface of a liquid into the Vapor state is called evaporation. Evaporation occurs more readily with

Increased temperature- more molecules have sufficient kinetic energy to overcome intermolecular forces of attraction in the liquid.
increased Surface Area of the liquid- a greater proportion of the liquid molecules are at the surface.
decreased strength of intermolecular forces- the kinetic energy needed to overcome the intermolecular forces of attraction is less, and more molecules have enough Energy to escape.
When Hydrogen Bonds are present, the Enthalpy of evaporation and the Boiling Point increase with the number of hydrogen bonds. When they are not, the enthalpy and the boiling point tend to increase with the molecular Polarizability.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/12-Intermole.title: Freezing Point
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/12-Intermole.content:
Definition
The Temperature at which Freezing occurs is called the freezing point. The Melting Point of a Solid and the freezing point of a Liquid are identical. At this temperature, solid and liquid coexist in equilibrium.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/12-Intermole.title: Freezing
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/12-Intermole.content:
Definition
The conversion of a Liquid to a Solid is called freezing, and is the Reverse Process of Melting.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/12-Intermole.title: Hydrogen Bond
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/12-Intermole.content:
Definition
The hydrogen bond is a specialized, relatively strong Dipole Dipole Attraction between a hydrogen Atom Covalently Bonded to a highly Electronegative atom  (\ce{N}, \ce{O}, \ce{F})

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/12-Intermole.title: London Forces
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/12-Intermole.content:
Definition
London forces are weak, temporary Van Der Waals Forces acting between every Atoms and Molecules, caused by fluctuations in electron density that create transient dipoles. The London forces become stronger as Polarizability increases.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/12-Intermole.title: Melting Point
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/12-Intermole.content:
Definition
The Temperature at which Melting occurs is called the melting point.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/12-Intermole.title: Melting
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/12-Intermole.content:
Definition
In a crystalline Solid, there is a regular, ordered arrangement of particles. That may be Atoms, Ions or Molecules. As a crystalline solid is Heated, its particles vibrate more vigorously. Eventually a Temperature is reached at which these vibrations disrupt the ordered structure. The particles can slip past one another and the solid loses its definite shape and is converted to a Liquid. This process is called melting.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/12-Intermole.title: Phase Diagram
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/12-Intermole.content:
Definition
A phase diagram is a graphical representation of the conditions of Temperature and Pressure at which Solids, Liquids and Gases (Vapors) exist, either as single State of Matter or as two or more phases in Equilibrium with one another.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/12-Intermole.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/12 Intermolecular Forces/State of Matter.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/12-Intermole.title: State of Matter
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/12-Intermole.content:
Definition
States of matter are distinct forms- Solid, Liquid Gas and Plasma, in which Matter exists based on molecular arrangement and Energy Levels . Solids have fixed Volume , liquids have fixed volume but flow, gases fill their container, and plasmas are ionized, high-Energy fluids. Phase changes occur with Temperature/Pressure changes.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/12-Intermole.title: Sublimation
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/12-Intermole.content:
Definition
Like Liquids, Solids can also give off Vapors, although because of the stronger Van Der Waals Forces present, solids are generally not as volatile as liquid at a given Temperature. The direct passage of Molecules from the solid to the vapor state is called sublimation.
When sublimation and Deposition occur at equal rates, a Dynamic Equilibrium exists between a solid and its vapor. The vapor exerts characteristic Pressure called the sublimation pressure.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/12-Intermole.title: Surface Tension
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/12-Intermole.content:
Definition
Surface tension, (\gamma) is the Energy, or Work required to increase the Surface Area of a Liquid. It has the units of energy per unit area, Joules per square meter (Jm^{-2}). As the Temperature increases, Van Der Waals Forces become less effective. Less work is required to extend the surface of a liquid.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/12-Intermole.title: Triple Point
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/12-Intermole.content:
Definition
The triple point is a special point on the Phase Diagram, that defines the unique Temperature and Pressure at which 3 States Of Matter, Solid, Liquid, and Gas, coexist in Equilibrium.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/12-Intermole.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/12 Intermolecular Forces/Van Der Waals Forces.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/12-Intermole.title: Van Der Waals Forces
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/12-Intermole.content:
Definition
The collective types of intermolecular Forces are known as van der Waals forces. The intermolecular forces contributing to the term a(\frac{n}{V})^2 in the van der Waals equation for nonideal gases are of this type.

Summary of Van Der Waals Forces

London Forces exist between all Molecules. They involve the Displacement of all the Electrons in molecules and they increase in strength with increasing Molecular Mass. The forces depend on molecular shapes.
Dipole Dipole Interactions involve displacement of elector pairs in Bonds and not molecules as a whole. These forces are found only in Substances with resultant Dipole Moments (Polar Molecules). Their existence adds to the effect of London forces also present.
When comparing substances of similar molecular size, dipole forces can produce significant differences in Properties.
When comparing substances of different molecular size, London forces are usually more significant than dipole forces.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/12-Intermole.title: Vapor Pressure
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/12-Intermole.content:
Definition
The Pressure exerted by a Vapor in a Dynamic Equilibrium with its Liquid is called the vapor pressure. Liquids with high vapor pressure at room Temperature are said to be volatile, and those with very low vapor pressure are called nonvolatile. The weaker the Van Der Waals Forces, the more volatile the liquid.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/12-Intermole.title: Vapor
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/12-Intermole.content:
Definition
A vapor is a Substance in the Gas phase at a Temperature lower than its Critical Temperature, which means that the vapor can be Condensed to a Liquid by increasing the Pressure on it without reducing the temperature of the vapor.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/12-Intermole.title: Viscosity
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/12-Intermole.content:
Definition
Viscosity is a Property partly related to Van Der Waals Forces, a Liquid resistance to flow. The stronger the intermolecular forces of attraction, the greater the viscosity. When a liquid flows, one portion of the liquid moves with respect to neighboring portions. Cohesive Forces within the liquid create an inter friction, which reduces the rate of flow. For liquids, viscosity decreases with increasing Temperature, but for Gases, the viscosity increases with increasing temperature.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/13-Entropy-a.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/13 Entropy and Gibbs Energy/13 Entropy and Gibbs Energy.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/13-Entropy-a.title: 13 Entropy and Gibbs Energy
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/13-Entropy-a.content:
Overview
Entropy, S, is a thermodynamic Property that is related to the way in which the Energy of a System is distributed around the available Energy Levels. A Microstate is a specific microscopic configuration describing how the particles of a system are distributed among the available energy levels. Boltzmann’s formula for entropy indicates that entropy is proportional to ln(W) where W is the number of microstates and, therefore, Boltzmann’s formula provides the basis for a microscopic view of entropy. For example, the spontaneous expansion of Ideal Gases involves an increase in entropy that can be rationalized in terms of an increase in the number of accessible energy levels and an increase in the number of microstates.
Clausius, using macroscopic observations, proposed that the entropy change for a process can be related to the amount of Heat transferred divided by the Temperature, provided the process is imagined to occur in a Reversible Way. Consequently, an entropy change, \Delta S, has the unit \frac{J}{K}. Clausius’s formula can be used to obtain expression for calculating entropy changes for a variety of physical changes, including phase transitions, constant Pressure Heating or cooling, the isothermal expansion or compression of an ideal gas.
A statement of the Third Law of Thermodynamics is that entropy of a pure perfect Crystal at 0 K is zero. Thus, we can assign a specific absolute value to the entropy of a pure Substance. This is marked contrast to the situation for other thermodynamic properties such as Internal Energy and Enthalpy, for which Absolute Values cannot be assigned. The absolute entropy of one Mole of substance in its Standard State is called the Standard Molar Entropy, S^{\circ}. Standard molar entropies of Reagents and Products can be used to calculate the Standard Reaction Entropy, \Delta _r S^{\circ}.
The basic criterion for Spontaneous Process is that the entropy change of the universe, which is the sum of entropy change of the system and its Surroundings, must be greater than 0. This statement is known as the Second Law of Thermodynamics. An equivalent criterion applied to the system alone is based on a thermodynamic function known as the Gibbs Energy, G. For an isothermal process, the Gibbs Energy Change, \Delta _r G, is the enthalpy change for the system minus the product of the temperature and entropy change for the system: \Delta _r G = \Delta H - T \Delta S.
The Standard Gibbs Energy of Reaction, \Delta _r G^{\circ}, is based on the conversion of Stoichiometric amounts of reagents in their standard states to stoichiometric amounts of produces in their standard states. Values of \Delta _r G^{\circ} are often calculated from tabulated values of Standard Gibbs Energies of Formation, \Delta _f G^{\circ} at room temperature. For nonstandard conditions, the Gibbs Energy of Reaction. \Delta _r G = \Delta _r G^{\circ} + RT \ln Q, where Q is the Reaction Quotient, takes account of the initial conditions. The value of \Delta _r G can be used to predict the direction of spontaneous change. The relationship between the standard Gibbs energy change and the Equilibrium Constant for a Chemical Reaction is: \Delta _r G^{\circ} = -RT \ln K. The constant K is the value of the reaction quotient Q at equilibrium and is called the thermodynamic Equilibrium Constant. Both Q and K are expressed in terms of the activities of reagents and products. The activities can be related to Molarities and gas partial pressures by means of a few simple conversion. The direction of spontaneous changes can also be predicted by comparing the values of Q and K.
Nonspontaneous Processes can be made spontaneous by coupling them with spontaneous reactions and by taking advantage of the State Function property of G. Coupled Reactions are paired reactions that yield a spontaneous Overall Reaction, occur in metallurgical processes and in biochemical transformations.
G.N, Lewis introduced the concept of chemical potential, represented by \mu and the concept of activity, a. The Chemical Potential of a substance refers to its ability or potential change the Gibbs energy of the system. The activity is defined in a way that ensures that the chemical potential has a specific form. The criterion for predicting the direction of spontaneous change can be obtained by considering the Gibbs energy of a Mixture, which can be expressed in terms of the chemical potentials of the substances involved.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/13-Entropy-a.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/13 Entropy and Gibbs Energy/Boltzmann Constant.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/13-Entropy-a.title: Boltzmann Constant
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/13-Entropy-a.content:
Definition
The Boltzmann constant, k_B is related to the Gas Constant and Avogadro’s Number.
k_B = \frac{R}{N_A}
