Chemistry/General-Chemistry/13-Entropy-a.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/13 Entropy and Gibbs Energy/Coupled Reactions.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/13-Entropy-a.title: Coupled Reactions
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/13-Entropy-a.content:
Definition
We have seen 2 ways to obtain Product from a Nonspontaneous Reaction:

Change the Chemical Reaction conditions to ones that make the reaction Spontaneous. (mostly by changing the Temperature)
Combine a pair of reactions, one with a positive Gibbs Energy Change and one with a negative \Delta _r G, to obtain a spontaneous overall reaction.
Such paired reactions are called coupled reactions.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/13-Entropy-a.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/13 Entropy and Gibbs Energy/Entropy.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/13-Entropy-a.title: Entropy
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/13-Entropy-a.content:
Definition
Entropy, S, is a thermodynamic Property that is related to the way in which the Energy of a System is distributed among the available Energy Levels.
Boltzmann associated the number of energy levels in the system with the number of ways of arranging the particles (Atoms, Ions or Molecules) in these energy levels. He derived the relationship
S = k_B \, ln(W)
Variables

























SymbolMeaningUnitsSEntropy(\frac{J}{K})k_BBoltzmann Constant(\frac{J}{K})Wnumber of Microstates
Summary of situations that produce an increase in entropy

Pure Liquids or liquid Solutions are formed from Solids.
Gases are formed from either solids or liquids.
The number of Molecules of gas increases as a result of a Chemical Reaction.
The Temperature of a Substance increases.

The entropy change for the surroundings in determined by the total amount of Heat that flows into the surroundings and the Temperature of the surroundings.
\Delta S_{surr} = \frac{-q_{sys}}{T_{surr}}

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/13-Entropy-a.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/13 Entropy and Gibbs Energy/Gibbs Energy Change.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/13-Entropy-a.title: Gibbs Energy Change
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/13-Entropy-a.content:
Definition
The Gibbs energy change, \Delta G, for a process at constant Temperature T is
\Delta G = \Delta H - T \Delta S
All the terms refer to changes for the System. All reference to the surroundings has been eliminated.
\Delta G = -T \Delta S_{univ}
By noticing that \Delta G is negative when \Delta S_{univ} is positive, we have the final criterion for spontaneous change based on Properties of only the system itself.

If \Delta G < 0, the process is a Spontaneous Process.
If \Delta G > 0, the process is a Nonspontaneous Process.
If \Delta G = 0, the process is a Reversible Process and the system has reached Equilibrium.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/13-Entropy-a.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/13 Entropy and Gibbs Energy/Gibbs Energy.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/13-Entropy-a.title: Gibbs Energy
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/13-Entropy-a.content:
Definition
Imagine a hypothetical process that occurs at constant Temperature T and constant Pressure P, with Work limited to Pressure Volume Work. We will assume that the surroundings also have temperature T. Because the pressure is constant we have \Delta H_{sys} = q_pBy the Entropy equation, the entropy change in the surroundings is
\Delta S_{surr} = -\Delta H_{sys} T
Substitute this value in the Second Law of Thermodynamics
T \Delta S_{univ} = T \Delta S_{sys} - \Delta H_{sys}
Cleaning the equation we get
-T \Delta S_{univ} = \Delta H_{sys} - T \Delta S_{sys}
The right side of this equation has terms involving only the System. On the left side appears the term \Delta S_{univ}, which embodies the criterion for spontaneous change, that for a Spontaneous Process is positive. Lets introduce a new thermodynamic State Function, called the Gibbs Energy, G.
The Gibbs energy for a system is defined by the equation
G = H - TS

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/13-Entropy-a.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/13 Entropy and Gibbs Energy/Microstate.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/13-Entropy-a.title: Microstate
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/13-Entropy-a.content:
Definition
Microstate is a specific microscopic Electron Configuration describing how the Atoms of a System are distributed among the available Energy Levels.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/13-Entropy-a.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/13 Entropy and Gibbs Energy/Second Law of Thermodynamics.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/13-Entropy-a.title: Second Law of Thermodynamics
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/13-Entropy-a.content:
Definition
All Spontaneous Processes produce an  increase in the Entropy of the universe.
\Delta S_{univ} = \Delta S_{sys} + \Delta S_{surr} > 0

If \Delta S_{univ} > 0, the process is spontaneous.
If \Delta S_{univ} < 0, the process is a Nonspontaneous Process.
If \Delta S_{univ} = 0, the process is a Reversible Process.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/13-Entropy-a.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/13 Entropy and Gibbs Energy/Standard Molar Entropy.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/13-Entropy-a.title: Standard Molar Entropy
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/13-Entropy-a.content:
Definition
The absolute Entropy of one Mole of Substance in its standard State of Matter is called the standard molar entropy, S ^\circ. Standard molar entropy increases as the number of Atoms per Molecule increases.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/13-Entropy-a.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/13 Entropy and Gibbs Energy/Standard Reaction Entropy.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/13-Entropy-a.title: Standard Reaction Entropy
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/13-Entropy-a.content:
Definition
The standard reaction entropy, \Delta _r S ^\circ, of a Chemical Reaction can be calculated using the Standard Molar Entropy for each Product and Reagent.
aA + bB + ... \rightarrow cC + dD + ...
When the uppercase letters represent different Substances and the lowercase letters represent the Stoichiometric Coefficients required to balance the Chemical Equation. \Delta_r S ^\circ for the reaction is obtained using the following equation.
\Delta _r S ^\circ = [c S_C ^\circ + d S_D ^\circ + ...] - [a S_A ^\circ + b S_B ^\circ + ...]

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/14-Solutions.title: 14 Solutions
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/14-Solutions.content:
Overview
In a Solution, the Solvent, usually the component present in greatest amounts, determines the State of Matter in which the solution exists. A Solute is a solution component dissolved in the solvent. Dilute Solution contain relatively small amounts of solute and Concentrated Solution, large amounts.
Any description of the Composition of a solution must indicate the quantities of solute and solvent present. Solution Concentrations expressed as Mass percent, Volume percent and mass/volume percent all have practical importance, as to the units, parts per million, ppm, parts per billion, ppb, and parts per trillion, ppt. However, the more fundamental concentration units are Mole fraction, Molarity and Molality. Molarity (moles of solute per liter of solution) is Temperature dependent, but mole fraction and molality (moles of solute per kilogram of solvent) are not.
Prediction about whether 2 Substances will mix to form a solution involve knowledge of Van Der Waals Forces between like and unlike Molecules. This approach makes it possible to identify an Ideal Solution, one whose Propertiescan be predicted from properties of the individual solution components. Most solutions are nonideal.
Generally, a solvent has limited ability to dissolve a solute. A solution containing the maximum amount of solute possible is a Saturated Solution. A solution with less than this maximum amount is an Unsaturated Solution. Under certain conditions a solution can be prepared that contains more solute than a normal saturated solution, such solutions are called Supersaturated. Solubility refers to the concentration of solute in a saturated solution and depends on temperature. Graphs of solute solubility versus temperature can be used to devise conditions for recovering a pure solute from a solution of several solutes through Recrystallization.
The solubilities of Gases depend on Pressure as well as temperature, and many familiar phenomena are related to gas solubilities. Henry’s Law relates the concentration of a gas in a solution to its pressure above the solution.
The Vapor Pressure of a solution depends on the vapor pressure of its pure components. If the solution is ideal, Raoult’s Law can be used to calculate the solution vapor pressure. Liquid Vapor Equilibrium curves showing either solution vapor pressures or solution Boiling Points as a function of solution composition help us visualize Fractional Distillation, a common method of separating the volatile components of a solution. Such curves also illustrate the formation of azeotropes in some nonideal solutions. Azeotropes are solutions that Boil at constant temperature and produce vapor of the same composition as the liquid. They have boiling points that in some cases are greater than the boiling points of the pure components and in some cases, less.
Osmosis is the Spontaneous flow of solvent through a semipermeable Membrane separating 2 solutions of different concentration. The net flow is from the less to the more concentrated solution. Osmotic flow can be stopped by applying a pressure, called the Osmotic Pressure, to the more concentrated solution. In Reverse Osmosis, the direction of flow is reversed by applying a pressure that exceeds the osmotic pressure to the more concentrated solution. Both osmosis and reverse osmosis have important practical applications. Osmotic pressure can be calculated with a simple relationship resembling the Ideal Gas Equation. Colligative Properties are certain properties that depend only on the concentration of solute particles in a solution, and not on the identity of the solute. Vapor pressure lowering is one such Property, and osmotic pressure is another.
Freezing Point depression and boiling point elevation are colligative properties having many familiar practical applications. For reasonably dilute solutions, their values are proportional to the molarity of the solution. The proportionally constants are K_f and K_b respectively. Historically, freezing point depression was a common method for determining Molar Mass.
Calculating colligative properties of Electrolyte Solutions is more difficult than for solution of Nonelectrolytes. The solute particles in electrolyte solution are Ions or ions and Molecules. Calculations using equations must be based on the total number of particles present, and the van’t Hoff factor is introduced into these equations to reflect this number. In all but the most dilute solutions, composition must be in terms of activities, effective concentrations that take into account interionic forces.
Colloids are an important intermediate state between a true solution and a Heterogeneous Mixture. Colloidal mixtures are responsible for some unusual phenomena and are encountered in a broad range of contexts, from fluids in living organisms to pollutant in large air masses.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/14-Solutions.title: Concentrated Solution
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/14-Solutions.content:
Definition
A concentrated solution is a type of Solution that has a relatively large quantity of dissolved Solute in a relatively small amount of Solvent.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/14-Solutions.title: Concentration
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/14-Solutions.content:
Definition
Concentration measures the amount of Solute dissolved in a specific Volume or Mass of Solvent/Solution.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/14-Solutions.title: Dilute Solution
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/14-Solutions.content:
Definition
Like Concentrated Solution, a dilute solution is a type of Solution that has a relatively small quantity of dissolved Solute in a relatively large amount of Solvent.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/14-Solutions.title: Enthalpy of Solution
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/14-Solutions.content:
Definition
In the formation of some Solutions, Heat is given off to the surroundings, in other cases heat is absorbed. We can figure out the enthalpy of solution in 3 steps.

Solvent Molecules must be separated from one another to make room for the Solute molecules. Some Energy is required to overcome the Van Der Waals Forces between solvent molecules. This step is an Endothermic Reaction, \Delta H > 0.
The solute molecules must be separated from one another. This step is also endothermic.
At last, we imagine that the solvent and solute molecules are attracted to one another. Therefore, when separated solvent and solute molecules combine to form a solution,, we expect energy to be released. This is an Exothermic Reaction.

The enthalpy of solution is the sum of all 3 Enthalpy changes.
\Delta _{soln} H = \Delta H_1 + \Delta H_2 + \Delta H_3
When the solute and solvent are both Liquids, \Delta H_1 is equal to \Delta _{vap} H, the enthalpy of Evaporation for the solvent and \Delta H_2 is equal to \Delta _{vap} H for the solute.
When the solute and solvent are Solids, than \Delta H_1 = \Delta _{sub} H, the enthalpy of Sublimation for the solvent and \Delta H_2 = \Delta _{sub} H for the solute.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/14-Solutions.title: Henry's Law
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/14-Solutions.content:
Definition
Henry’s law states that the Solubility of a Gas increases with increasing Pressure.
C = k \times P_{gas}
Henry’s law applies only to Equilibrium between Molecules of a Gas and the same molecules in Solution.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/14-Solutions.title: Heterogeneous Mixture
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/14-Solutions.content:
Definition
If  Van Der Waals Forces between unlike Molecules are much weaker than those between like molecules, the components remain segregated in a heterogeneous mixture.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/14-Solutions.title: Homogeneous Mixture
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/14-Solutions.content:
Definition
A homogeneous mixture is a type of Mixture that combines 2 or more Substances that is uniform throughout, possessing the same Composition and Properties regardless of where the sample is taken. All Solutions are homogeneous because the dissolved Solute is present throughout the solution.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/14-Solutions.title: Ideal Solution
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/14-Solutions.content:
Definition
If the Van Der Waals Forces are of the same type or of equal strength, the Solute and Solvent Molecules mix randomly. A homogeneous Mixture or Solution appears. Because Properties of solution of this type can be predicted from the properties of the pure components, they are called ideal solutions. There is no overall Enthalpy change in the formation of an ideal solution, \Delta _{soln} H = 0.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/14-Solutions.title: Molality
Nonideal Solution
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/14-Solutions.content:
Definition
If the Van Der Waals Forces between unlike Molecules are more attractive than those between like molecules, a Solution forms. The Properties of such solutions cannot be predicted, however, they are called nonideal solutions. Interactions between Solute and Solvent molecules release more Heat that the heat absorbed to separate the solvent and solute molecules. The solution process is an Exothermic Reaction, \Delta _{soln} H < 0.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/14-Solutions.title: Recrystallization
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/14-Solutions.content:
Definition
Recrystallization is a technique for purifying Solid Compounds by dissolving them in a hot Solvent and allowing pure Crystals to reform upon cooling, leaving impurities dissolved in the Liquid.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/14-Solutions.title: Saturated Solution
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/14-Solutions.content:
Definition
A saturated solution is a Mixture containing the maximum Concentration of a dissolved Solute in a Solvent at a specific Temperature and Pressure. At this point, no additional solute will dissolve, and any excess added will remain undissolved or settle at the bottom. It represents a state of Dynamic Equilibrium between dissolved and undissolved solute.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/14-Solutions.title: Solubility
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/14-Solutions.content:
Definition
The Concentration of the Saturated Solution is called the solubility of the Solute in the given Solvent. Solubility varies with Temperature.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/14-Solutions.title: Supersaturated Solution
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/14-Solutions.content:
Definition
A supersaturated solution is a type of Solution that is unstable, in a nonequilibrium state, containing more dissolved Solute that the maximum amount that can normally be dissolved in a Solvent at a given Temperature.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/14-Solutions.title: Unsaturated Solution
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/14-Solutions.content:
Definition
An unsaturated solution is a Mixture that contains less dissolved Solute than the maximum amount the Solvent can hold at a specific Temperature and Pressure. Because it has not reached its Saturation Point and can become a Saturated Solution.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/15-Chemical-.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/15 Chemical Equilibrium/15 Chemical Equilibrium.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/15-Chemical-.title: 15 Chemical Equilibrium
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/15-Chemical-.content:
Overview
When a Chemical Reaction is carried out in a closed reaction vessel at constant Temperature T, the System proceeds Spontaneously toward Equilibrium. At equilibrium, the Reaction Quotient Q attains the same constant value K. Mathematically, the equilibrium condition is expressed as
Q = K. An important Property of the equilibrium state is that it is Dynamic: The forward and reverse reactions continue to occur at equal rates after equilibrium is reached.
This condition of dynamic equilibrium is described through an Equilibrium Constant, K. The form of the equilibrium constant is established from the balanced Chemical Equation using activities. The thermodynamic equilibrium constant is unitless, although in most applications, we do not explicitly include the units.
When the equation for a Reversible Process is written in the reverse order, the equilibrium constant is inverted from its original form. When 2 or more reaction are Coupled together, the equilibrium constant for the Overall Reaction is the product of the K values of the individual reactions. The equilibrium constant of a reaction can have different values depending on the reference state used. For K_c , a Concentration reference state is used, while for K_p , a Pressure reference state is used.
The magnitude of the equilibrium constant can be used to determine the outcome of a reaction. For large K values the reaction goes to completion, with all Reagents converted to Products. A very small K, for example, a large negative power of 10, indicates that practically none of those reagents have been converted to products. Finally, equilibrium constant of an intermediate value between 10^{-10} and 10^{10}, indicate that some of the reagents have been converted to products.
A comparison of the reaction quotient with the equilibrium constant makes it possible to predict the direction of net change leading to equilibrium.

If Q < K, the forward reaction is favored, meaning that when equilibrium is established the amounts of products will have increased and the amount of reagents will have decreased.
If Q > K, the reverse reaction is favored until equilibrium is established.
If Q = K, neither the forward nor reverse reaction is favored. The initial conditions are in fact equilibrium conditions.

Le Chatelier’s Principle is used to make qualitative predictions of the effect of different variables on an equilibrium condition. This principle describes how an equilibrium condition is modified in response to the addition or removal of reagents are changes in reaction Volume, external Pressure or temperature. Catalysts, by speeding up the forward and reverse reactions equally, have no effect on an equilibrium condition.
For quantitative equilibrium calculations, a few basic principles and algebraic techniques are required. A useful method employs a tabular system, called the ICE table, for keeping track of the initial concentrations of the reagents and products, changes in these concentrations and the equilibrium concentrations.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/15-Chemical-.title: Equilibrium Constant
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/15-Chemical-.content:
Definition
The equilibrium constant, K, is a numerical value defining the ratio of Product Concentration to Reagent concentration for a Reversible Process at Equilibrium, with each concentration raised to the power of its Stoichiometric Coefficient. It indicates whether products (K > 1) or reagents (K < 1) are favored at a given Temperature.
For the general Chemical Equation aA + bB \ce{\leftrightharpoons} cC + dD, the equilibrium constant is expresses as
K = \frac{[C]^c [D]^d}{[A]^a [B]^b}
When individual equations are combined, their equilibrium constants are Multiplied to obtain the equilibrium constant for the Overall Reaction.
A reaction goes essentially to completion if K > 10^{10} and not at all if K < 10^{-10}.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/15-Chemical-.title: Equilibrium
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/15-Chemical-.content:
Definition
A System at equilibrium is in a state of balance. macroscopically, the Composition of the system is unchanging whereas, at the microscopic level, change continues. The overall composition of the system does not change because, at equilibrium, a balance has been achieved between 2 opposing processes. The conversion of small amounts of Reagents into Products is perfectly offset by the conversion of small amounts of products into reagents. This balance maintains the lowest possible value for the Gibbs Energy of the system and the maximum possible value for the combined Entropy of the system and its surroundings. Unless disturbed by an external influence, the system remains indefinitely in this equilibrium state.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/15-Chemical-.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/15 Chemical Equilibrium/Le Chatelier's Principle.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/15-Chemical-.title: Le Chatelier's Principle
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/15-Chemical-.content:
Definition
Le Chatelier’s principle means that when an Equilibrium System is subjected to a change in Temperature, Pressure, or Concentration of a reacting species, the system responds by attaining a new equilibrium that partially offsets the impact of the change.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/15-Chemical-.title: Reaction Quotient
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/15-Chemical-.content:
Definition
The reaction quotient, Q, is a measure of the relative amounts of Products and Reagents present in a Chemical Reaction at any given time, calculated using the same formula as the Equilibrium Constant, but with instantaneous Concentrations. Comparing Q to K determines the direction a reaction will shift to reach Equilibrium:

Q < K proceeds forward forming more products
Q > K proceeds backward forming more reagents
Q = K at equilibrium

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/16-Acids-and.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/16 Acids and Bases/16 Acids and Bases.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/16-Acids-and.title: 16 Acids and Bases
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/16-Acids-and.content:
Overview
The Bronsted Lowry theory describes an Acid as a Proton Donor and a Base as a Proton Acceptor. In an Acid-Base Reaction, the base takes a Proton (\ce{H+}) from an acid. In general, acid-base reactions are Reversible. The Conjugate Base (\ce{A-}) is derived from the acid \ce{HA} whereas the Conjugate Acid \ce{HB+} is derived from the base \ce{B}. The combination of \ce{HA/A-} and \ce{B/HB+} are known as Conjugate Acid-Base Pairs. The conjugate acid of Water is the Hydronium Ion, \ce{H3O+}. Certain Substances, for example water, are said to be Amphiprotic. They can act as an acid or a base.
In pure water and in Aqueous Solutions, Self Ionization of the water occurs to a very slight extent, Producing \ce{H3O+} and \ce{OH-}, as described by the Equilibrium Constant K_w , known as the Ion Product of Water. The designations pH and pOH are often used to describe the Concentrations of \ce{H3O+} and \ce{OH-} in aqueous solutions.
The equilibrium constant for the Chemical Reaction of an acid with water is called the Acid Ionization Constant K_a , and that for the reaction of a base with water is called the Base Ionization Constant K_b . Strong Acids and Strong Bases have large ionization constants and are essentially completely Ionized in water. Weak Acids and Weak Bases have small ionization constants and ionized to a limited extent in water. The extent to which acids or bases ionize in water is described in terms of either the Degree of Ionization \alpha, or the Percent Ionization. For a weak acid or base, the degree of ionization increases with increasing Dilution.
In aqueous solutions, strong acids ionize completely to produce \ce{H3O+} and strong bases Dissociate completely to produce \ce{OH-}.
Weak acid or base ionizes to a limited extent in water. The extent of their ionization can be related to the ionization constants K_a and K_b or their logarithmic equivalents pKa and pKb by setting up and solving an equilibrium calculation. Calculations involving ionization equilibria are in many ways similar to those in 15 Chemical Equilibrium, although some additional considerations are necessary for Polyprotic Acids.
Polyprotic acids are acids with more than one ionizable \ce{H} Atom that undergo a stepwise ionization and have a different ionization constant, K_{a_1}, K_{a_2}, ... , for each ionization step.
In certain situations, it may be necessary to consider 2 or more ionization reactions. A general approach for handling such situations involves writing down all equilibrium constant expressions, 1 or more material balance equations and a charge balance equation. A material balance equation indicates that the equilibrium concentrations of all forms of a given acid or base must be equal to the initial or stoichiometric concentration of the acid or base. The charge balance equation indicates that the solution carry no net Charge.
In reactions between Ions and water- Hydrolysis reactions, the ions react as weak acid or bases. the pH of Salt solutions depends on the Anions and/or Cations present. Anions from weak acids act as bases whereas cations from weak bases act as acids.
For an acid-base reaction, Equilibrium favors the formation of the weaker acid and the weaker base. If the acid or base in an acid-base reaction is strong, then the reaction goes essentially to completion.
Molecular Composition and structure are the keys to determining whether a Substance is acidic, basic or amphiprotic. In addition, molecular structure affects whether an acid or base is strong or weak. In assessing acid strength, factors that affect the strength of the Bond that must be broken to release \ce{H+} must be considered. Alternatively, factors that affect the stability of the anion formed by the acid can be considered. In assessing base strength, factors that affect the ability of Lone Pair Electrons to bind a proton are of primary concern.
The Lewis acid-base theory views an electron-pair acceptor as a Lewis Acid and an electron-pair donor as a Lewis Base. The addition Compound of a Lewis acid-base reaction is referred to as an Adduct. The theory is most useful in situations that cannot be described by means of proton transfers, for example, in reaction involving Gases and Solids and in reaction between organic compounds.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/16-Acids-and.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/16 Acids and Bases/Acid Ionization Constant.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/16-Acids-and.title: Acid Ionization Constant

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/16-Acids-and.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/16 Acids and Bases/Acid-Base Reaction.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/16-Acids-and.title: Acid-Base Reaction
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/16-Acids-and.content:
Definition
Acid-base reaction is a Chemical Reaction where an Acid and a Base react to neutralize each other, typically Producing Water and Salt. The reaction involves a transfer of Protons from the acid to the base  (Bronsted Lowry theory), or exchange of Ions, resulting in a pH change toward neutrality.

For an acid-base reaction, Equilibrium favors the formation of the Weaker Acid and the Weaker Base.
If the acid or base in an acid-base reaction is Strong Acid or Strong Base, they react essentially to completion.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/16-Acids-and.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/16 Acids and Bases/Adduct.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/16-Acids-and.title: Adduct
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/16-Acids-and.content:
Definition
The Product of an Lewis Acid-Base Reaction is called an adduct.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/16-Acids-and.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/16 Acids and Bases/Amphiprotic.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/16-Acids-and.title: Amphiprotic
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/16-Acids-and.content:
Definition
Amphiprotic species are chemical Substances that can both Donate and Accept a Proton, allowing them to act as either a Bronsted Lowry Acid or Base depending on the Reaction. Water is an example of an amphiprotic Molecule.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/16-Acids-and.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/16 Acids and Bases/Base Ionization Constant.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/16-Acids-and.title: Base Ionization Constant
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/16-Acids-and.content:
Definition
The base ionization constant, K_b , is the Equilibrium Constant for the Ionization of a Weak Base in Water, measuring the strength by quantifying its Dissociation into Conjugate Acid and hydroxide Ions (\ce{OH-}). A higher K_b value indicates a Stronger Base

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/16-Acids-and.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/16 Acids and Bases/Bronsted Lowry theory.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/16-Acids-and.title: Bronsted Lowry theory
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/16-Acids-and.content:
Definition
The Bronsted Lowry theory defines Acids as Proton Donors and Bases as Proton Acceptors. This theory is fundamental for understanding acid base Reactions, specifically focusing on the transfer of Protons between species.

An acid contains at least one Ionizable \ce{H} Atom, and a base contains an atom with a Lone Pair of Electrons onto which a proton can bind.
For a Conjugate Acid Base Pair, the Molecular Formula for the acid and base differ by a single proton.
When added to Water, acids Protonate water Molecules to form hydronium (\ce{H3O+}) Ions and bases Deprotonate water molecules to form hydroxide (\ce{OH-}) ions.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/16-Acids-and.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/16 Acids and Bases/Conjugate Acid Base Pair.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/16-Acids-and.title: Conjugate Acid Base Pair
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/16-Acids-and.content:
Definition
A conjugate acid base pair consists of two Substances that differ only by one Proton (\ce{H+}), as defined by the Bronsted Lowry theory. An Acid becomes its Conjugate Base after donating a proton. A Base becomes its Conjugate Acid after accepting a proton.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/16-Acids-and.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/16 Acids and Bases/Conjugate Acid.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/16-Acids-and.title: Conjugate Acid
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/16-Acids-and.content:
Definition
A conjugate acid is a chemical species formed when a Bronsted Lowry Base Accepts a Proton. It is a Product of a base gaining a hydrogen Ion, effectively acting as an Acid in the reverse Reaction by being capable of Donating that proton back.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/16-Acids-and.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/16 Acids and Bases/Conjugate Base.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/16-Acids-and.title: Conjugate Base
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/16-Acids-and.content:
Definition
A conjugate base is a chemical species formed when a Bronsted Lowry Acid Donates a Proton during a Chemical Reaction.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/16-Acids-and.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/16 Acids and Bases/Degree of Ionization.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/16-Acids-and.title: Degree of Ionization

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/16-Acids-and.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/16 Acids and Bases/Hydrolysis.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/16-Acids-and.title: Hydrolysis
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/16-Acids-and.content:
Definition
The Chemical Reaction between an Ion and Water is called a hydrolysis. In it water is used to break down Chemical Bonds within a Molecule, splitting it into smaller components. It involves adding a hydrogen Ion (\ce{H+}) to one fragment and a hydroxyl Group (\ce{OH-}) to another.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/16-Acids-and.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/16 Acids and Bases/Ion Product of Water.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/16-Acids-and.title: Ion Product of Water
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/16-Acids-and.content:
Definition
The ion product of water, K_w , is the Equilibrium Constant for the Self Ionization of Water into hydronium (\ce{H3O+}) and hydroxide (\ce{OH-}) Ions, expressed as
K_w = [\ce{H+}] [\ce{OH-}]
At room Temperature, this constant is 1.0 \times 10^{14} mol^2 dm^{-6} , where the Concentration of both \ce{H+}, \ce{OH-} in pure water is 1.0 \times 10^{-7} M.
-\log K_w = pK_W= pH + pOH

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/16-Acids-and.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/16 Acids and Bases/Lewis Acid.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/16-Acids-and.title: Lewis Acid
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/16-Acids-and.content:
Definition
A Lewis acid is a species (an Atom, Ion, or Molecule) that is an Electron pair acceptor.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/16-Acids-and.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/16 Acids and Bases/Lewis Base.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/16-Acids-and.title: Lewis Base
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/16-Acids-and.content:
Definition
A Lewis base is a species (an Atom, Ion, or Molecule) that is an Electron pair donor.
A Chemical Reaction between a Lewis Acid and Lewis base results in the formation of a Covalent Bond between them.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/16-Acids-and.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/16 Acids and Bases/Polyprotic Acid.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/16-Acids-and.title: Polyprotic Acid
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/16-Acids-and.content:
Definition
Polyprotic acid is an Acid capable of Donating more than one Proton per Molecule in a stepwise manner.
They Ionize in stages, with each subsequent step having a smaller Acid Ionization Constant.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/16-Acids-and.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/16 Acids and Bases/Self Ionization.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/16-Acids-and.title: Self Ionization
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/16-Acids-and.content:
Definition
Self ionization is a Chemical Reaction where 2 identical Molecules, commonly Water, Collide and transfer a Proton to form Ions.

The self ionization of water is partially suppressed by the addition of Acid or Base to water.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/16-Acids-and.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/16 Acids and Bases/Water.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/16-Acids-and.title: Water
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/16-Acids-and.content:
Definition
Water is an inorganic Compound with the Chemical Formula \ce{H2O}. It is a transparent, tasteless, odorless and nearly colorless chemical Substance. It acts as a Liquid Solvent.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/16-Acids-and.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/16 Acids and Bases/pH.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/16-Acids-and.title: pH
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/16-Acids-and.content:
Definition
pH is the potential of hydrogen Atom. It is define by as the negative of the logarithm of the Concentration of \ce{H+}. pH = -\log [\ce{H3O+}]

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/16-Acids-and.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/16 Acids and Bases/pKa.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/16-Acids-and.title: pKa
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/16-Acids-and.content:
Definition
The pKa is defined as the negative logarithm of the Acid Ionization Constant.
pK_a = -\log K_a

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/16-Acids-and.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/16 Acids and Bases/pKb.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/16-Acids-and.title: pKb
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/16-Acids-and.content:
Definition
The pKb is defined as the negative logarithm of the Base Ionization Constant.
pK_b = -\log K_b

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/16-Acids-and.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/16 Acids and Bases/pOH.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/16-Acids-and.title: pOH
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/16-Acids-and.content:
Definition
The quantity pOH can be defined as pOH = -\log [\ce{OH-}]

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/17-Acid-Base.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/17 Acid-Base Equilibria/17 Acid-Base Equilibria.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/17-Acid-Base.title: 17 Acid-Base Equilibria
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/17-Acid-Base.content:
Overview
The Ionization of a Weak Electrolyte is suppressed by the addition of an Ion that is the Product of the ionization and it is known as the common ion effect. This effect is a manifestation of Le Chatelier’s Principle.
Buffer Solution is a Solution that resist changes in pH upon the addition of small amounts of an Acid or Base. The finite amount of acid or base that a buffer solution can neutralize is known as the Buffer Capacity, and the pH range over which the buffer solution neutralizes the added acid or base is the Buffer Range. Calculating the pH of a buffer solution can be accomplished by using the Henderson Hasselbalch Equation.
Substances whose colors depend on the pH of a solution are known as Acid-Base Indicators. They exist in solution as a Weak Acid and its Conjugate Base. Each form has a different color. The pH range over which an acid-base indicator changes color is determined by the Acid Ionization Constant.
The Concentration of an acidic or basic solution of known concentration can be determined by Titration with a base or acid of known concentration. In this process the Volume of the solution of known concentration, the Titrant, is added through a burette into a measured quantity of the unknown, Analyte in a beaker. The point at which neither Reagent is in excess in a titration is known as the Equivalence Point. The End Point can be located through the change in color of the indicator.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/17-Acid-Base.title: Acid-Base Indicator
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/17-Acid-Base.content:
Definition
An acid-base indicator is a Substance whose color depends on the pH of the Solution to which it is added. Acid-base indicators exist in two forms:

A Weak Acid, represented symbolically as \ce{HIn} and having one color.
Its Conjugate Base, represented as \ce{In-} and having a different color.
When just a small amount of indicator is added to a solution, the indicator does not affect the pH of the solution. Instead, the Ionization Equilibrium of the indicator is affected by the \ce{[H3O+]} in solution.


From Le Chatelier’s Principle, we see that increasing \ce{[H3O+]} in a solution displaces the equilibrium to the left, increasing the proportion of \ce{HIn} and the Acid color.
pH = pK_{\ce{HIn}} + \log \frac{[\ce{In-}]}{[\ce{HIn}]}

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/17-Acid-Base.title: Analyte
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/17-Acid-Base.content:
Definition
An analyte is a Substance that is of interest in an analytical procedure of Titration.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/17-Acid-Base.title: Buffer Capacity
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/17-Acid-Base.content:
Definition
Buffer capacity refers to the amount of Acid or Base that a Buffer Solution can neutralize before its pH changes. The maximum buffer capacity exists when the Concentration of a Weak Acid and its Conjugate Base are kept large and equal to each other.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/17-Acid-Base.title: Buffer Range
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/17-Acid-Base.content:
Definition
The buffer range is the pH range over which a Buffer Solution effectively neutralizes added Acids and Bases and maintain a constant pH.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/17-Acid-Base.title: Buffer Solution
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/17-Acid-Base.content:
Definition
A buffer solution is a type of Solution that resists significant changes in pH upon the addition of small amounts of Strong Acid or Strong Base, maintaining a stable, relatively constant pH. They are Composed of a Weak Acid and its Conjugate Base, or a Weak Base and its Conjugate Acid.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/17-Acid-Base.title: End Point
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/17-Acid-Base.content:
Definition
The point in a Titration at which the Acid-Base Indicator changes color is called the end point. The end point must match the Equivalence Point if the neutralization.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/17-Acid-Base.title: Equivalence Point
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/17-Acid-Base.content:
Definition
The equivalence point is the precise moment in a Titration when the added Titrant Chemically Reacts completely with the Analyte.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/17-Acid-Base.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/17 Acid-Base Equilibria/Henderson Hasselbalch Equation.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/17-Acid-Base.title: Henderson Hasselbalch Equation
Titrant
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/17-Acid-Base.content:
Definition
A titrant is a Solution of precisely known Concentration, added slowly from a burette to a sample (Analyte) during Titration to determine the analyte’s concentration. It acts as a Reagent that react quantitatively with the analyte until the Reaction’s End Point is reached.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/17-Acid-Base.title: Titration
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/17-Acid-Base.content:
Definition
Titration is a laboratory method used to determine the unknown Concentration of a target Solution (Analyte) by adding a Reagent of known concentration Titrant from a burette. The process continues until the Reaction reaches completion, indicated by a color change (End Point).
For equal Volumes of Acid solutions of the same Molarity, the volume of Base required to titrate to the Equivalence Point is independent of the strength of the acid.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/18-Solubilit.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/18 Solubility Equilibria/18 Solubility Equilibria.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/18-Solubilit.title: 18 Solubility Equilibria
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/18-Solubilit.content:
Overview
The Equilibrium Constant for the Equilibrium between a Solid Ionic Solute and its Ions in a Saturated Solution is expressed through the Solubility Product Constant, K_{sp}.
A solute’s Molality in a saturated Aqueous Solution is known as its molar solubility. Molar solubility and K_{sp} are related to each other in a way that makes it possible to calculate one when the other is known.
The Solubility of a slightly soluble ionic solute is greatly reduced in an aqueous solution containing ion in common with the solubility equilibrium- a common ion.
The solubility product concept is most useful for slightly soluble ionic solutes, and especially in cases when activities can be replaced by Molar Concentrations. Moderately or highly soluble ionic compounds require the use of activities. The presence of common ions reduces the solubility of a sightly soluble ionic solute, generally to a significant degree. Other factors also affect solute solubility. The presence of noncommon or diverse ions generally increases solute solubility, an effect called the Salt Effect. Solute activities, and hence solute solubilities, are strongly influenced by interionic attractions, which become especially significant at higher concentrations and for highly charged ions. Dissociation of ionic solute may not be 100% complete, leading to the formation of Ion Pairs which act as a single units.
To determine whether a slightly soluble solute will Precipitate from a solution, the Ion Product Q_{sp} is compared with the solubility product constant. Q_{sp} is based on the initial ion concentrations in a solution. K_{sp} , on the other hand, is based on the equilibrium ion concentration in a Saturated Solution. If Q_{sp} > K_{sp} , precipitation will occur. If Q_{sp} < K_{sp} , the solution will remain Unsaturated. When Q_{sp} = K_{sp}, the solution is just saturated.
A comparison of K_{sp} values is a factor in determining the feasibility of Fractional Precipitation, a process in which one ionic species is removed by precipitation while others remain in solution.
The solubility of a slightly soluble solute is affected by pH if the Anion is \ce{OH-} or derived from a Weak Acid. The solubility increases as the pH lowered or decreases as the pH is raised. This can be illustrated through Le Chatelier’s Principle. Also, an equilibrium constant for the dissolution Reaction can be obtained by combining the solubility equilibrium equation and the ionization equilibrium equation of the Weak Electrolyte. Some slightly soluble solutions form Suspensions, which are Heterogeneous fluids containing solid particles that will eventually settle.
A Complex Ion is a polyatomic ion Composed of a Central Metallic Solids bonded to 2 or more Molecules called ligands. The formation of complex ion is an equilibrium process with an equilibrium constant called the Formation Constant, K_f. In general, if the formation constant is large, the concentration of uncomplexed metal ion in equilibrium with the complex ion is very small. Complex ions formation can render certain insoluble materials quite soluble in appropriate aqueous solutions. A complex ion is either a Cation or an anion depending upon the particular central metal ion and the particular ligands. When a complex ion and an oppositely Charged ion combine they form a Coordination Compound.
Precipitation, Acid-Base, Oxidation Reduction, and complex ion formation Reactions are all used extensively in Qualitative Cation Analysis. Such an analysis can provide a rapid means of determining the presence or absence of certain cations in an unknown material.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/18-Solubilit.title: Complex Ion
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/18-Solubilit.content:
Definition
A complex ion is polyatomic Cation or Anion Composed of a Central Metal Ion to which other groups (Molecules or ions) called ligands are Bonded.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/18-Solubilit.title: Coordination Compound
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/18-Solubilit.content:
Definition
Coordination compounds are Substances containing Complex Ions. Theses complexes from through Lewis Acid-Base Reaction and often exhibit distinct vibrant colors, specific magnetic Properties (Paramagnetic or Diamagnetic) and diverse Geometries. The coordination number is the number of Donor Atoms directly Bonded to the Central Metal (commonly 4 or 6).

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/18-Solubilit.title: Formation Constant
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/18-Solubilit.content:
Definition
The formation constant K_f, of a Complex Ion is the Equilibrium Constant describing the formation of a complex ion from a Central Ion and its attached groups (Molecules or ions). One feature that distinguishes K_f from other equilibrium constants is that K_f values are usually large numbers.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/18-Solubilit.title: Fractional Precipitation
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/18-Solubilit.content:
Definition
Fractional precipitation is a technique in which 2 or more Ions is Solution, each capable of being Precipitated by the same Reagent, are separated by the proper use of that reagent: One ion is precipitated while the other(s) remains in solution. The primary condition for a successful fractional precipitation is that there be a significant difference in the Solubility of the Substances being separated. The key to the technique is the slow addition of a Concentrated solution of the precipitating reagent to the solution from which precipitation is to occur, as from a burette.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/18-Solubilit.title: Ion Pairs
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/18-Solubilit.content:
Definition
Ion pairs are distinct, electrostatically bound Complexes of a Cation and an Anion that behave as a single entity in Solution without forming Covalent Bonds. They form when Ions do not completely Dissociate, often in Solvents with low dielectric constants, and act as an intermediate state between Ionic and neutral species.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/18-Solubilit.title: Ion Product
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/18-Solubilit.content:
Definition
The ion product Q_{sp}, is the product of the Molar Concentration of Ions in a Solution at any given moment, calculated similarly to the Equilibrium Constant. It is used to determine if a Precipitate will form Q > K, if the solution is Saturated Q = K, or Unsaturated Q < K

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/18-Solubilit.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/18 Solubility Equilibria/Qualitative Cation Analysis.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/18-Solubilit.title: Qualitative Cation Analysis
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/18-Solubilit.content:
Definition
An analysis that aims at identifying the Cations present in a Mixture is called qualitative cation analysis. It provides us with many examples of Precipitations, Equilibria, Acid-Base Equilibria and Oxidation Reduction Reactions.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/18-Solubilit.title: Salt Effect
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/18-Solubilit.content:
Definition
The salt effect refers to how adding Salts to a Solution alerts the reaction rates (kinetic salt effect) or Solubility (solubility salt effect) by increasing the solution’s Ionic Strength

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/18-Solubilit.filePath: Chemistry/General Chemistry/18 Solubility Equilibria/Solubility Product Constant.md
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/18-Solubilit.title: Solubility Product Constant
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/18-Solubilit.content:
Definition
The solubility product constant, K_{sp} , is the Equilibrium Constant for the dissolution of a Solid Ionic Compound into its Ions in a Saturated Solution. It equals the product of the Molar Concentration of the ions, each raised to the power of its Stoichiometric Coefficient, indicating a Compound Solubility.
The solubility of a sightly soluble ionic compound is lowered in the presence of a second Solute that furnishes a common ion.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/18-Solubilit.title: Suspension
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/18-Solubilit.content:
Definition
The pH of a Solution can affect the Solubility of a Salt to a large degree. That is especially true when the Anion of the salt is the Conjugate Base of a Weak Acid or the base \ce{OH-} itself. A suspension is a Heterogeneous Fluid containing Solid particles that are sufficiently large for sedimentation and, unlike Colloids, will settle.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/19-Electroch.title: 19 Electrochemistry
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/19-Electroch.content:
Overview
In an Electrochemical Cell, Electrons in an Oxidation Reduction Reaction are transferred at Metal strips called Electrodes and conducted through an external circuit. The Oxidation and Reduction Half-Cell reactions occur in separated regions called half-cells. In a half-cell, an electrode is immersed in a Solution. The electrodes of the 2 half-cells are joined by a wire, and an electrical connection between the solutions is also made, as through a Salt Bridge. The cell reaction involves oxidation at one electrode called the Anode and reduction at the other electrode called the Cathode. A Voltaic Cell produces Electricity from a Spontaneous redox reaction. The Cell Voltage is the Potential difference (Voltage) between the 2 electrodes, designated as E_{cell}. A Cell Diagram displays the components of a cell in a symbolic way.
The reduction occurring at a Standard Hydrogen Electrode, is arbitrarily assigned a Potential of 0. A half-cell has a Standard Electrode Potential, E^{\circ}, in which all Reagents and Products are at unit activity. A half-cell reaction with a positive standard electrode potential than does reduction of \ce{H+} Ions at the standard hydrogen potential. A negative standard electrode potential signifies a lesser tendency to undergo reduction. The Standard Cell Potential, E_{cell}^{\circ}, of a voltaic cell is the difference between E^{\circ} of the cathode from the E^{\circ} of the anode.
Cell voltages based on standard electrode potentials are E_{cell}^{\circ} values. The electrical Work that can be obtained from a cell depends on the number of Electrons involved in the cell reaction, the cell potential, and the Faraday Constant F, which is the number of coulombs of Charge per Mole of electrons- 96485 \frac{c}{mol}. An important relationship exists between E_{cell}^{\circ} and \Delta _r G^{\circ}, the Standard Gibbs Energy of Reaction, namely, \Delta _r G^{\circ} = -z F E_{cell} ^{\circ}. The Equilibrium Constant of the cell reaction K is related to E_{cell} ^{\circ} through the expression \Delta _r G^{\circ} = -RT \ln K = -z F E_{cell}.
In the Nernst Equation, E_{cell} for nonstandard conditions is related to E_{cell} ^{\circ} and the Reaction Quotient Q. If E_{cell} > 0, the cell reaction is Spontaneous in the forward direction for the stated conditions. If E_{cell} < 0, the forward reaction is Nonspontaneous for those conditions. A Concentration Cell consists of 2 half-cells with identical electrodes but different solution Concentrations.
An important application of voltaic cells is found in various battery systems. A Battery stores Chemical Energy so that it can be released as Energy. Batteries consist of one or more voltaic cells and are divided into 4 major classes: Primary Cell, Secondary Cell, Reverse Battery and Fuel Cell in which reagents such as hydrogen and oxygen, are continuously fed into the battery and chemical energy is converted to Electrical Energy.
Electrochemistry plays a key role in corrosion and its control. Oxidation half-cells reactions product anodic regions and reduction half-cells reactions cathodic regions. Cathodic Protection is achieved when a more active metal is attached to the metal being protected from corrosion. The more active metal, a “sacrificial” anode, is preferentially oxidized while the protected metal is a cathode at which a harmless reduction half-cell reactions occurs.
In Electrolysis, a nonspontaneous Chemical Reaction occurs as electrons from an external source are forced to flow in a direction opposite that in which they would flow spontaneously. The electrochemical cell in which electrolysis is conducted is called an Electrolytic Cell. E^{\circ} values are used to establish the theoretical voltage requirements for an electrolysis. Sometimes, particularly when a Gas is liberated at an electrode, the voltage requirement for the electrode reaction exceeds the value of E^{\circ}. The additional voltage requirement is called the Overpotential. The amount of reagents and products involved in an electrolysis can be calculated from the amount of electric charge passing through the electrolytic cell. The Faraday constant is featured in these calculations.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/19-Electroch.title: Anode
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/19-Electroch.content:
Definition
If Oxidation takes place, the Electrode is called the anode. It is a Metal strip.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/19-Electroch.title: Battery
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/19-Electroch.content:
Definition
A battery is a device that stores Chemical Energy for later release as Electricity (Matter possessing Charge). Some batteries consist of a single Voltaic Cell with 2 Electrodes and the appropriate Electrolytes. An example is a flashlight cell. Other batteries consist of 2 or more voltaic cells joined in series- plus to minus, to increase the total Voltage. An example is an automobile battery.
There are 3 types of voltaic cells and the batteries based on them are:

Primary Cell
Secondary Cell
Reverse Battery
Fuel Cell

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/19-Electroch.title: Cathode
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/19-Electroch.content:
Definition
If Reduction takes place, the Electrode is called the cathode. It is a Metal strip.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/19-Electroch.title: Cathodic Protection
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/19-Electroch.content:
Definition
Cathodic protection is an electrochemical technique to prevent corrosion by making a Metal surface the Cathode of a Cell, forcing it to stop Oxidation. It protects submerged or buried metallic structures by using sacrificial Anodes to feed Electrons to the protected structure, ensuring it remains inert.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/19-Electroch.title: Cell Diagram
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/19-Electroch.content:
Definition
A cell diagram shows the components of an Electrochemical Cell in a symbolic way. It has the following general form:

The arrow indicates the direction of Electron flow in an external circuit.
We will use the following generally accepted conventions in writing cell diagrams:

The Anode, the Electrode at which Oxidation occurs, is placed at the left side of the diagram.
The Cathode, the electrode at which Reduction occurs, is placed at the right side of the diagram.
A boundary between different phases (for example, an electrode and a Solution) is represented by a single vertical line (|).
The boundary between Half-Cell compartments, commonly a Salt Bridge, is represented by a double vertical line (||). Species in Aqueous Solution are placed on either side of the double vertical line. Different species within the same solution are separated from each other by a comma.
When appropriate, Concentrations, Pressures or activities for each species are given in parentheses.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/19-Electroch.title: Cell Voltage
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/19-Electroch.content:
Definition
The cell voltage, E_{cell} is the electric Potential difference between the 2 Electrodes (Anode and Cathode) of an Electrochemical Cell, Voltage representing the Force that drives Electrons through an external circuit. Measured in volts (V), it acts as a measure of Energy per Charge, often determined by subtracting the anodic potential from the cathodic potential.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/19-Electroch.title: Concentration Cell
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/19-Electroch.content:
Definition
A concentration cell consists of 2 Half-Cells with identical Electrodes but different Ion Concentrations. Because the electrodes are identical, the Standard Electrode Potentials are numerically equal and subtracting one from the other leads to the value. However, because the ion concentrations differ, there is a Voltage between the 2 half-cells. The Spontaneous Process in a concentration cell always occur such that the concentrated Solution becomes more Dilute, and the dilute solution becomes more concentrated. The final result is as if the solutions were simply mixed. In a concentration cell, however, the natural tendency for Entropy to increase in a mixing process is used as a means of producing Electricity.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/19-Electroch.title: Electrochemical Cell
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/19-Electroch.content:
Definition
The properly connected combination of 2 Half-Cells is called an Electrochemical Cell. It a device that generates Electrical Energy from Spontaneous Oxidation Reduction or uses electrical energy to drive Nonspontaneous redox reactions. It consists of an Anode and a Cathode immersed in Electrolyte Solution, usually connected by a Salt Bridge.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/19-Electroch.title: Electrode
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/19-Electroch.content:
Definition
When used in electrochemical studies, a strip of Metal, \text{M} is called an electrode. 2 kinds of interactions are possible between metal Atoms on the electrode and metal Ions in Solution:

A metal ion \ce{M^n+} from solution may Collide with the electrode, gain n Electrons from it, and be converted to a metal atom \text{M}. The ion is Reduced.
A metal atom M on the surface may lose n electrons to the electrode and enter the solution as the ion \text{M}^{n+}. The metal atom is Oxidized.
An Equilibrium is quickly established between the metal and the solution, which can be represented as \text{M}(s) \xrightleftharpoons[\text{reduction}]{\text{oxidation}} \text{M}^{n+}(aq) + ne^-

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/19-Electroch.title: Electrolysis
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/19-Electroch.content:
Definition
The process in which a Nonspontaneous Process is driven by the application of Electrical Energy to split Compounds into Elements. It involves an Electrolyte, a Cathode (negative Electrode) attracting Cations and an Anode attracting Anions.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/19-Electroch.title: Electrolytic Cell
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/19-Electroch.content:
Definition
The electrolytic cell is a type of Electrochemical Cell that uses Electricity to produce a Nonspontaneous Process. It converts Electrical Energy into Chemical Energy to decompose Compounds (Electrolysis).

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/19-Electroch.title: Faraday Constant
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/19-Electroch.content:
Definition
When a Reaction occurs in a Voltaic Cell, the cell does Work. Think of this as the work of a moving electric Charges. The total work done is the product of 3 terms:

Cell Voltage, E_{cell}.
n, the number of Moles of Electrons transferred between the Electrodes.
The electric charge per mole of electrons called the Faraday Constant, F = 96485 \frac{C}{mol}.
W_{elec} = nFE_{cell}

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/19-Electroch.title: Fuel Cell
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/19-Electroch.content:
Definition
Fuel cells are Voltaic Cells that materials (Reagents, Products and Electrolytes) pass through them, which is simply a converter of Chemical Energy to Electrical Energy. These types of Batteries can be run indefinitely as long as they are supplied by electrolytes.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/19-Electroch.title: Half-Cell
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/19-Electroch.content:
Definition
An Electrode immersed in a Solution containing Ions of the same Metal, \text{M}^{n+}, is called a half-cell.

Chemistry/General-Chemistry/19-Electroch.title: Nernst Equation
Chemistry/General-Chemistry/19-Electroch.content:
Definition
The Work that can be derived from a process is equal to the negative Gibbs Energy Change. For an electrochemical Reaction, we have n = z \xi , where z is the electron number, the Atomic Number + Absolute Value of negative Charge. \xi is the extent of reaction in Moles. Substituting, we get:
W_{elec} = - \Delta G = z \xi F E_{cell}
The quantity \Delta G / \xi is the Gibbs energy change per mole of reaction, represented as \Delta _r G.
\Delta _r G = -z F E_{cell}
From the Gibbs Energy of Reaction, Standard Gibbs Energy of Reaction, and the Reaction Quotient, Temperature and the Gas Constant we get: \Delta _r G = \Delta _r G^{\circ} + RT \ln Q
Substituting, we get:
-z F E_{cell} = -z F E_{cell}^{\circ} + R T \ln Q
Dividing through by -z F gives the Nernst equation:
E_{cell} = E_{cell}^{\circ} - \frac{RT}{zF} \ln Q
